LATER, SAME DAY

Rolling along through England on one of their ® mpartment ~
trains. Remarkable how smooth these big wheeled cars are. The rugzed=
ness has disavpeared and now the beauty is one of gently rolling hills,
a few scattered scraggly trees which are clumped but rarely; of no com-
mercial value, butall add to the beauty of the country. These green
hills are checker-boarded by low hedge or stone fences which separate
each farmer's plot, one plated for oats, the other for frazing, another
for small vegetables and all of a different color in our moving vanor-
ama. |

The homes are mactically all stone or brick = much brick, and
all are nest and clean, Amazing to find a neat little stone cottage
with flower and vegetable gardens along the railroad track, where in
our country only dirty shacks would be found. The stock, cattle,horses
and sheep all look exceptionally healthy. As we move from the country
into a village or citv, a forest of chimnies greets us. E’ ch stone
house has four to eight chimnies and each chimney has three to six
stacks. Apparently each room has a fireplace. Children run all over
the place, and thev and their elders ereet us for the first time with
the finger "v" made famous by ChurchHill, They all seem poorly clothed
and many ragged, asthey run up to the train to ask for candy or gum.
We have been warned not to give anything to them or toss them anything,
for a few have been killed lately as they have been lured into the path
of a passing train by a penny stick of gum.

The Ked Cross has again greeted us and apparently are doing
a swell job over here, At the dock ve were served coffee and dough-
nuts by American girls - twelve of them - and at our first stop had
coffee and doughnuts.

Played bridge this morning with Jessie Barnett, one of your
motor corvs girls who left Ann Arbor in Junee Whe was secretary at
the J. A. G. school for several months. She ceme across with us and

surely was excited about being here, but has no idea whet her assigne

AUGUST 29
SOMEWHERE IN ENGLAND

Well located now in barracks and in fine old camr. It is an
old cavalry camp and in its day must have been a beauty, but too many
American feet have trod its halls in recent vears and worn out the poor
old wooden stairs. Shower6& are complete absent and bathtubs a rarity;
when we do take one, we are limited to a five-inch tub of water. We
shave in bowls, sleep in double deck bunks, have no rugs and so have
all the conveniences of a farmhouse at home.

In our room are six officers: Captains Bamford, Crayton,
Terrel and myself, Lts. Lees and Haakana. We will probably manage to
have a chummy little game of bridee from time to time. We eat xifmt in
our barracks and so far the meals have been fine, wlthough the serving
is poorly organized. ‘Ye have a bar where we can get British beer which
tastes like a poor batch of home made root beer. However, the water
is not safe in many plases to drink and the advice is to learn to like
it. Our equipment is fine end coming along in good shape. I wish I
could tell you about it. ,

The English "bit" and "bob" are cradually yielding to my
mastery, but I will probably be rooked plenty before I leave here. The

kids are the sharp ones.

SEPTEMBER 14

Firday # almost another week, and we are still here. ‘We have been
busy getting everything ready, our equipment, and trying to devise a
way to take it, and that keeps me busy. Occasionally a bridge game in
the evening or a bicycle ride, but in zeneral it has been too cold.
You ask about Christmas. I can't think of much. Air mail envelopes
are at a vremium. Don't send razor blades. If the Free Press sends
V-mail, 0.K. - otherwise,no. I have lost my wool toaue end am unable

to get another. Would like to go back to London.

Bristol is a very nice place and harder hit than I had anti-

Its back away from the coast and the Avon river there is too shallow for

opened again and traffic can continue. In that part of the country you

mountain top we could see the complete wall encircling the

mountains are topped by houses or castles. How they do love
to put a house on top of a rock.

air with just room enough for about an 8 room house-=-and

home, but sitting on top of this rock overlooking the town
and little stream.

feeling. Many French,Russians and Poles left behind and quite
a good number of Jerries. Of the latter a few are cooperative,
or try to be, but can't be trusted and many are sullen and
quite objectionable. They are haughty even in defeat, but

seem glad that it is "about over",

Their bandages are many of them paper and their bandages in
general of inferior quality. Their adhesive tape is excellent,
better than ours, and their instruments and some other equipment
is very good.

Recently, talked with some wounded Jerry P.W.'s as
they rode in our ambulance. One asked if we had heard of their
50 man tanks. I eyed him and thought I caught a glitter there.
We gulped and said "no", ‘Sure," said he, "one to drive, one to
fire, and 48 to push it!" The air corps has done a terrific
job in eliminating their gasoline.

As we go along the towns are filled with Czecks, Poles
and Russians, etc. who were the slave laborers around here. We
have passed several camps of theirs and they file down the road
in groups or singly--headed "home", Their job is unlimited also.
Any who were in their particular Army snap to attention to give
a beautiful salute to practically all of our vehicles--they are
saluting their liberators. One old gent with a red handlebar

One Serbian officer, a student of eight languages
really wanted to come with us. He was in good health in spite of
his years around here and merely asked for a gun and permission

them to get some meat.

Several of your letters handy so will glance them over
for questions, Major Baker has left us, goto Surgeon's office
in Paris. Hopes to get on a Surgical team. He was the first
Med. officer across the bridge. Your word about the V.R. of the

certainly think well of you and your work, Perhaps it is because
you can type now eh???

hardly worth the difference. We are getting blades in good shape
now too. Supply is wonderful-miraculous. Glad the book arrived
O.K. Look up Schyondweiler and Ermsdorf vicinity. Vivid Christmas
recollections.

ous. Rather heavily wooded with beautiful trees. Really the
more I see of this country and its beauties (nature not feathles)

far the furthest advanced of the countries we have seen so far, and
although the present towns have their manure piles, the larger
towns and cities are quite modern. Would gladly trade it for a
promenade on State Street though.

us up. That night we heard you firing and swing southof ------ Licpyy
(he named the city but I can't for censorship reasons) and
we really prayed. As we started out the next morning, that
was this morning, a Frenchie came up and told us 6 killometers.
Well, we thought, "shall we wait for them? Can we make the
guards?" Then we saw your dust ahead and to our right. We
couldn't realize what it was. "Must be Jerries", we thought.

They can't be the Americans. But we sat down and told the guards
we were going no farther for those were Americans. They took
off like scared rabbits, and about thattime one of your tanks
came flying under a railroad bridge and began to fire on us.
They didn't recognize us at first, and I am not surprised, but
we really took to the ditches, Then they stopved, and came
up along side of us and said "sorry boys, didn't know who you
were", Then they gave us all cigarettes. And well, I just
sat down and cried. He ground out his cigarette butt in our

A FORTUNE. We never wasted even a tiny butt like this. We
chatted a bit longer then went to bed.

APRIL 2h, 195

A quiet day and just came in from an interesting
spectacle. The Kraut family was sitting and standing around
in front of their house watching the sun setting beyond the
fields in front. The old man sat in his chair smoking his
pipe and looking intently at the activities in the field.

His daughter was standing behind him and his young son sat
on the fence. The white flag of their truce, which we have
seen so frequently of late, flapped over their heads.
Occasionally mother would stick her head out of the upstairs
window to watch the crazy Americans. They all sat or stood
there q@iunly looking toward the smokestacks of the city, but
interested in the field activities. And what were the G.I's
doing--playing baseball, laughing and yelling and running
wildly around they were playing good old softball while the
puzzled Krauts tried to figure it out almost symbolic.

Before ae Czeck friends I went with the
doctor back to their concentration camp and to the Panzerfaust
(Bonga) factory where they worked. Interesting to me and
probably it all left a queer feeling in his stomack to walk
back through buildings as a free man where but a few days
before he had been imprisoned. He worked there four months
loading boxes as a laborer before they put him to work as a
medic. He picked up a little canvas rod-like bag, about an
inch in diameter and two feet long filled with lead shot. He
handed it to me "TrRacihagers he said, "death beater". "They
left this behind, but used it when we disobeyed." I am sending

it home in my next box.

SOMEWHERE SOMETIME

This picture just came to my attention--and I liked
it.Why? It is as near to the way those dough medics, and ours
who are with the companies, look (at times) than any thing I
have seen. How those boys do take it!

I shall never forget our man Stella the morning after
Euskirchen. He and De Moss had been up until about 3:00 A.M.
bringing in wounded doughs. The dough medics were about
worked out and oursstill had their pep so off they went
through the mud and dark--and fire and they brought the men
in. Then Stella went to the next aid station bank and brought
up Plasma--through the same conditions. The next morning
the sm shone brightly and there was Stella. He looked at
me, something like this chap, the sparkle gone from his eyes
and replaced by honest fatigue. A three days beard blackened
his face. A silk scarf, once dainty, was fluffed around his
neck and knotted beneath his ching to help break the cold
wind. He was tired, but had to keep going and he knew it.
"Just reporting, captain," he said. I couldn't tell him to
go back, and didn't have to.

These boys don't have the relatively easy life we
do. They are with the companies all the time carrying their
Red Cross forward with their only weapon--the scissors on their
side. Snipers like these white circles with red crosses for
they make good targets. Still they keep going and want to
stay with the men they are working with. They won't quit and

Lord knows I sure admire them for it.

badges only for doughs--and our boys pick up as many or more

gone and will be left here when we leave. The rest are still
together although one carries on his hand the scar of a sniper
shot. These are the boys who do the work and take the beating

at the same time--God bess them.

UNDATED LETTER

Nothing new today. Am enclosing a copy, Mother,
of a letter I wrote to Mrs. Landre in answer to one from her
telling of an evening visit with a "friend". This chap was a
German architect who left Der Vaderland around 1907. Seemed to
be a bit of a Nazi sympathizer and aroused their ire a bit with
some of his discussions. This more or less summarizes my

feelings and activities along this line in recent weeks.

MAY 1, 1945, SOMEWHERE IN DER HINTERLAND

Your last letter telling of your argument with the
German "friend" of yours hit me at a most inopportune time. It
so happens that we have been working rather closely with many
of these "slaves" or "paid laborers" as your friend speaks of
them, both as they leave the farms where they work and as they
have come from the concentration camps. I have difficulty handling
the language myself, but in our small detechment are two Germans,
a Polish boy and two Italians all of whom can speak their native
tongue very freely. Through them I have pumped quite a few of
these people and they all have been more than free to talk.

In the first place it won't do any good to argue with
this fellows for the Germany he knew is entirely different than
the Germany of today, or I hope, of tomorrow. There have been
the changes of two wars around here since he was in Germany and
it is definitely the Germany of today that we are fighting (and

Back to the present. Working on the farm where we
are staying was a young Pole and his wife. They did all the farm
labor as the owner is an old coot with whiskers whose labor days
are, or were, over. Paid? Yes. She was paid 5 marks a week
(mark=roughly equal to 10 cents) and he a mark a day-=$1.20
a week for the two of them. (How much does your friend make?)
(And furthermore, why is he still where he is if this place is
so much better?) Room and board sures; one little attic room--
my men won't even sleep in it. And bord consisting mainly of
potatoes and potato pancakes, At one time they asked for better
food, and went on a starvation strike when it was denied.
Immediately the farmer got one of the local police who came
clamoring down here and proceeded to beat up the chap and his
wife. He took by far the worse beating and was unable to work
for some time. When the Jerries hands got sore he got a club
and finished it that way. They were never allowed out after
dark and when picked up after curfew hours a 50 mark (compare
with pay) fine was immediately and standardly clamped upon them.
If that was not deemed enough they were beat. I recently sent home
one of their cute little "todschlagers" which was used in camps
to keep them working. These Poles said that they were never
allowed to be sick, If anybody was sick he was immediately
sent off to the concentration camp nearby (and whose name would
be familiar to you if I could mention it) and seldom were ever

seen again. It is another destroying camp.

"In bondage", definately; but a type of human bondage
that is unbelievable. As long as they were of physical use and
value to the country they were allowed to exist, then like the
worn out horse were destroyed, when that stage was passed. No
attempt was made to keep families together. (The little Czech
doctor long ago lost track of his wife and child and the female
doctor in the same camp long ago lost track of her husband. )

Some time before we pounded our way into one of these industrial
towns a group of about 75 were deemed useless and definitely
harmful if captured by the Americans, They were marched out into
the woods a few kilometers from town and made to clear out a
space and then dig a huge hole to be their grave. A little
Italian slipped out and reported the story taking some of our
authorities with him. There he said the Krauts had whipped

and beat these people until they fell either dead, or nearly so,
into the hole. Then all was covered and concealment attempted.
Townspeople, including the burgermeister, were taken out there
and made to disinterr the bodies and rebury them in burlap

sacks each in a single grave. Nice business, being "in bondage"
to these friendly people!

so much by the horrors of war, because I expected that and was
prepared for it, but by the activities committed by the civilians,
the perpetual crimes committed by them in the name of "Der Feurer"
end the ease with which theyadmit what they did and yet pass it
off as nothing. Their minds are so twisted that they cannot
recognize right from wrong and have lost all respect for their
fellow humans. They gave no quarter yet are asking for not a
quarter, but the whole darned thing. They still think they are
supermen--even in defeat.

I am enclosing a picture of one of these supermen ,

a regimental commander, for Bill. It is not meant to be a pinup,
but I thought you might be interested in his hat and its insignia.
Personally the seat of his pants is just as attractive as his
face, and the ideas read behind those eyes of his.

But this is enough chater for one sitting. It will
give you pleasant dreams and perhaps a bit to toss back at your
friend. Give it to him with my regards, as well as your feeling,
and if I could buy him a ticket back here, I sure would. They

need architects!

Judging from the radio excitement and reports the lights went on
with a crash and the victory commotion is mainly a ringing of
bells and blaring of horns.

Here, oddly enough, it is different. All has been
strangely quiet for such a day. It is a day we have all looked
forward to for some time and now it is herewewell: The men went
around their customary duties. Though we have been out of the
line for some days the perpetual process of cleaning and mainte-
nance goes on. Very little wine and cognac flowed, although it
was available. Nobody was excited--in fact it is all a great
let down.

Why--well we all wonder what now. For most of us there
is but one answer: the job is only half done and real work is
now settling around us. If we remain here the problems are
immense. The personal problem of learning to live with people
whom we learned to dislike, to distrust and to kill will be but
one. The problem of reorienting them in world affairs of feed-
ing, clothing, housing and carring for them--you can't appreciate
it. The reestablishment of homes for the thousamis of "displaced
personel" of getting them back to where there home was. For
weeks we have seen these poor imm agrants wandering aimlessly
around and along the roads--toward the front and the Russians,
away from it to France and Belgium--and it continues. By day
they carry their earthly belongings on their back or putg them in
a wagon. By night they sleep in the fields or roads or ditches,

or if lucky curl in a barn with but one thought in mind--to travel.

J@ were met very gracefully by a KLM representative and there was a bus to

in New York unable to speak any English except to say, "I want to go to

New York." He had joined some friends in Misgouri, and.that fall he started
to learn English. A few months later he entered college, and three years
later he entered medical school. He has just now finished his internship
at Denver, and is returning home for the first time, He added a bit of
life to our trip. | fat ,

Shortly after noon the 5 of us took off by streetcar, and this time
we managed to get on the right end, bougnt our tickets, and rode down
to the "Dam Square." <A short block off of the "Dam Square" Walt
walked us to the FPleissig Hotel, where he stayed his one night in
Amsterdam last year while he was en route to England. Frankly I
think we are all much happier ia the little canal house Hotel DeMmoor
than we would be in such a‘ busy, bustling hotel, at least as we saw
it today. However, it was basically very nice, and as those of you
who have seen Walt's pictures may remember, this hotel has a lovely
dining room with old chandeliers and decorations.

From there we walked two or three blocks over to the West Church,
where Rembrandt is buried, and about two doors away was Ann Frank's
House. This, of course, was the oilgrimage that our youngsters were
particularly interested in,and since it had been closed when we were
there the other day we were most pleased to find it open today. It
frankly was quite an experience, and a very interesting Cescrintion |
was given by the guide that we all appreciated, but particularly our
three youngsters. Actually the quarters were larger than we had
anticipated. The whole escanade was well planned by Mr. Frank, hav~
ing been conceived and altered over a two-year period, with finally
the quiet shift into the back quarters leaving letters behind at their
home address saying they were going to France and Spain. Thus their
exodus from Amsterdam was not unusual, not unexpected, and they
actually were not sought after and probably.ynever would have been
found if someone hadn't "squealed on them." As a result of an unfor-
tunate informative phone call, however, the police visited their quar-
ters, searched around and moved behind the bookcase and discovered
their two-floor hideout, and they were all moved to concentration camps.
Subsequently, as you know, all died there except Mr. Frank. He later
returned to Amsterdam and found Ann's diary, and after much soul-
searching had it published, the results of which you are all familiar
with, He is now living in Basel, Switzerland, occasionally return-
ing to Amsterdam. ‘The Germans, after they had cleared the Franks and
their friends out of these quarters, had sent all of the furniture
back to Germany, aS was their custom. They dumped all the papers,
leaving them benind, and one of the friends of the Franks Lound the
oapers and saved them, including Ann's diary. She had actually read
the diarv, but sne was not sure whether she should give it to Mr.
Franks when he returned, for fear it would be most distressing to him.
However, finally she did give it to him, and the rest is known to his-
tory. This whole set-uo is now a non-profit making foundation aimed
basically at better understanding of the youth of the world, of all
nations and religions, and there is a small building next door avail-
able to these young people as housing quarters while in Amsterdam if
they so desire. It is apparently the seat of many philosophical dis-
cussions and meetings thoughout the year.

I am approaching the end of this tape and unfortunately mailed all
the rest of them ahead to Copenhagen, so I will not be able to finish
the remainder of our Amsterdam adventures at this time. Actually we
had a wonderful afternoon with Fritz, seeing a few other areas, and
then back here. Adios, a"

Dick

Ann speaking: Last Sunday we went to the Ann Frank House in
Amsterdam, which we found to be most interesting. The annex

which the Franks had was in the back of the building, where Mr.
Frank and Mr. Van Dan had their spice business. It consisted of

4 bedrooms, a kitchen, and an old restaurant. They moved into
this annex in 1942, and lived there for about two years until in
1944, when one German and 4 Dutch Nazi policemen suddenly stormed
upstairs and forced them to leave their annex. They were taken

to Auschwitz, the Nazi death camp in southern Poland. Everyone

in Ann's family, including herself, died in these concentration
camps except for Otto Frank, her father. He was freed in 1945,
Miet, his former typist, had been in their annex since they had
gone, and recovered some papers of Ann's, He did not know at this
time that this was her diary. Without reading them, he gave them
to Mr. Frank and he read them. Had Miet read them, he might not have
given them to him for reasons of safety. The diary is now written
in many different languages, including German, and several million
copies have been sold. Thousands of people go through the Ann
Frank House each year, but “the Ann Frank House is not a monument,
not a memorial--it is a summons to speak out, to listen, and to be
willing to hear." Also on Sunday we went to the church, Our Lord
in the Attic. The name of this church comes from its being built
on about the fourth, fifth and sixth floors of a house, Several of
these churches in the "attics" of houses were built just after the
Reformation, when the Catholics were driven from their churches and
compelled to worship in secret. Through time, all of the other
several hundred churches have been demolished, and now the Our Lord
in the Attic Church is the only one existing in Amsterdam. These
churches were not publicized, but those that did know about them
and were against them tolerated them. I particularly enjoyed the
architecture of it because it is older than any other church that I
have ever seen. I also found it very fascinating that they could
have the first three stories of a house look exactly like a house,
and then going up into the next story you would go up a stairway
and all of a sudden you would be in a gigantic church. For this
peemen: I found the church to be very unique, and enjoyed it all
the more,

In my last letter, I mentioned the confusion with our bags, which
were flown over on a later plane; but they finally came through,
and we picked them up later on Wednesday, our day of arrival, All
arrived in excellent shape.

Back to Sunday, the 26th, We walked home from the Ann Frank House,
completing our walk downtown and back. Our “dogs" were plenty
tired, Fritz picked us up with his Volkswagen and drove us around
for a couple of hours late Sunday afternoon, going past both the
old and the new church, However, we did not go into them, Ann
has already described Our Lord in the Attic Church, and has given
her impressions of that, We also stopped at a delightful little
section--Begi jnhof--which is a court of perhaps 30 homes for
elderly Catholic ladies. In other words, an old ladies’ home for
Catholic women. It was delightful, and quite a surprise to walk
into this quiet little court with its green grass, surrounded by
small Dutch canal-type homes, somewhat in miniature, and contain-
ing two churches--one a Catholic church, and the other an English
Presbyterian church, I have no explanation as to why the latter
ia there. Certainly with the flowers, the green grass, the quiet-
ness of the court, it is an excellent place for retirement. The
Begijnhof is the best-known of the many “hofjes" scattered through
emsterdam. These are all little collections of homes built by
socially conscious wealthy families of the 1600's and 1700's as
housing developments for the poor of Amsterdam--a social con-
sciousness long before our country.

We also went past “The Waag," which was a 17th century weighing
house with a circular interior and turreted exterior. Since
shortly before the war, it had been an historical museum; but

at least as far as I am concerned, the corner entranceway which
was, of course, closed--it being Sunday--with the words "“sur-
gical Amphitheater" over it, was the most Surprising and inter-~
esting feature, It was in this Surgical Amphitheater where the
dissections were done, and where Rembrandt did some of his well-
known paintings. Hla Avallreny Leeann ”

Of course, we had to go past the narrowest house in Amsterdan,
which is only one door wide, being built by a wealthy 17th cen-
tury merchant when his coachman one day unwittingly apparently
made the remark, "I'd be happy if I had a house as wide as your
front door." Hence the narrowest house, some four or five
stories high, but only one narrow door's width in breadth,

Not knowing when we would get our car, and frankly not expecting

to get it until Friday, I had made arrangements shortly after we
arrived for a man to drive us around north Denmark, With 5 of us,
this was actually cheaper than the bus "rubberneck" tour, and we
could set our own pace and see places that we wanted to gee; also
it allowed us to stop and take pictures as we wished. This worked
out excellently; so yesterday (Thursday) at 8:00 in the morning,
Our driver picked us up and we drove in luxury with a good American
Chrysler around northern Denmark! We went north from Copenhagen to
Hillerod, and then north to the coast at Hornbaek, through beautiful
Danish countryside. Kay will give you the details of this later,

We then followed the coast down to Bisingor, saw Hiamlet's castle, ~~

and took a hurried trip over to Ha xg, Sweden. This gave
us about an hour's wandering in the- shopping area there, much to
the delight of the women; I am not so sure that it was a good idea,
However, we all enjoyed it, and were glad to say that we had been,
even for a short time, in Sweden. We returned to Denmark, drove
down the coast, stopping at Deer Park, then had dinner at the
Bellevue Strand Hotel overlooking the harbor, One of my greatest
Surprises along this trip, incidentally, was the narrowness of
the isthmus between Elsingor and Halsingborg. Actually it did
not look much wider than the Detroit River, although it is about
twice as wide. This is particularly significant when one recalls
that this is the only entrance to the Baltic Sea, and the only
sea entrance to Russia. I had my first taste of smoked eel, and
found it delicious, Karl, our driver, had been talking about it
early in the day, and found that they had fresh smoked eel at
this dining area, so we both ordered it and he showed me how to
eat it. Actually it was delicious. We had had a sample at lunch,
as we ate in a little outdoor cafe at Hornbaek and had smorgasbord
there, but he did not tell us that it was eel until we had all
finished it, Then we admitted that its taste was most delicious.
It was late when we returned from this trip, 80 to bed and up
this morning,

Today we again had breakfast here in the hotel, and I had a
scrambled egg, which is the first non-soft boiled egg that I

have had since leaving the States, Actually it was more of an
omelet than a scrambled egg, but it sure tasted good. My camera
had been acting up, and yesterday went completely on the fritz;
and since I am lost without a camera, we changed our plans regard-
ing buying a movie camera over here and I have purchased a new

35 mm. By the time-Walt and I were through shopping for this

with its lenses, and taking a trial roll of film so that it

could be processed today, we found ourselves into the early
afternoon, German cameras, incidentally, are actually cheaper
here in Denmark than they are in Germany; and at least we under-
stand the Germans come up here to buy cameras while the Danes go
to Germany to buy radios and tape recorders. This is because of
their tax play between countries, and the established set prices
for cameras in Germany. This latter change has taken place appar-
ently only in the last 6 months; so at least at the moment it
would appear that cameras were cheaper right here. Certainly the
camera that I purchased was much cheaper than if I had bought it

This is Walt talking now, sitting in my hotel room in Hamburg,
Germany, trying to relate facts of something that we saw 4 week

ago in southern Holland, This concerns our trip to the Delta
region of the Rhine and Maas Rivers, just south of Rotterdam out-
side of a little town of Haringvliet. A 20 25-minute boat

ride from this town took us to an artificial reated island in
the middle of the mouth of this river. On this |island, which was
constructed in 1958, are now 17 water locks, known as sluices,
which will hold back the sea water from the fresh water of the
rivers, the Rhine and the Maas. The island is about 1 mile long,
and about a quarter of a mile wide, The sluices were started in
1962 and completed earlier this year. The sluices actuallyrare i
water locks. ‘There are 17 of these, with two gates in each one~~
one gate facing the sea, and one gate facing the fresh water of

the river mouth, Standing inside of these locks, which have not
yet been opened for the water (they are still completing them),

you feel like a speck of dust. These gates are 3 or 4 stories
tall, and weigh 250 tons each, They are raised at a speed of

1 cm. per second, and they will be raised and lowered 3 or 4

times a day when the water in the river will be higher than the
water in the sea, so the fresh water will run to the sea. ‘This

have been at least 30 miles an hour, and everybody came back just
soaked; but we all feel it was well worth it. The basic advantages

large flood in this area around the Rhine River, when many lives

again. As we visited just as tourists, we really cannot feel the
total effect of this project; but it is certainly amazing to see
what they have done in merely 13 years since this flood, and what
they have planned to do in the next 10 years to dam off this whole
area. And just walking and viewing this whole project, you really
don't see how they could have done it, it's such an amazing project
and such a large undertaking, especially for such a small country
as Holland, really. This is due to be coppleted around 1930--the
whole project including the dykes--although they have the major
part of it completed now with these sluices completed. For the
outside work, they did not have the engines actually working yet,
but these will be finished soon. Within the next year they will
have water in these sluices, although they will not be serving the
purpose intended until around 1980, After leaving the project, we
came back into Rotterdam. We drove through Rotterdam, and saw the
area that was destroyed during World War II and is now rebuilt,

In back of the house, they have a very pleasant garden which Mrs,
Dekking keeps up nicely. The fronts of the houses, although old,
are decorated with gables at the top. Each gable is different,
and in the olden days this took the place of the house numbers
that we use today. One thing that would be hard on Americans in
these houses is that usually there are Only 3 bathrooms and they are
a couple of floors apart; you would have to be running up and

down to get to them. The Ginners, as mentioned, were very lovely.
They were very big and filling. Before each meal, Mrs, Dekking
prepared soup--homemade, of course--that was delicious, One thing
interesting is that everybody drank wine--even their l2=year old
son, Edward, This is not out of the Ordinary. The dessert, as
best I can describe it, was a building of calories! While we were
at the Dekkings', Doctor Dekking's mother was there, and she was a
very charming woman, She was about the age Of 87, and a talker,
She presently lives in Rotterdam, so “everything is Rotterdam. ¥
She is a wonderful woman, and very witty for her age. On Tuesday,
June 28, we went to the Diamond Cutters', which is the largest
permanent diamond exhibition in the world, This factory was built
in 1889, and modernized after World War Ii, It is very interesting
to see how a diamond is cut and then polished to a beautiful gem.
At the end, they had a selection of diamond bracelents, clips and
earrings that were fun to look at, but naturally expensive to buy.
From there, we walked in the rain to Rijksmuseum to get there just
as it opened, It proved very beneficial, This museum is known
worldwide, and we could certainly see why, The paintings are more
than beautiful. This museum is represented by the finest works of
both old and new contemporaries. The most famous paintings there
were by Rembrandt, They were lovely, and so realistic with light-
ing effects, His most famous painting, The Night Watch, was fab-
ulous to look at. It is an Outstanding work of art, and will long
be remembered, I am sure, by all of us. Another great picture by
Rembrandt is The Holy One, which has tremendous lighting effects
and was very enlightening. There was a lot for us to grasp in the
short time we were there, but it was very worthwhile. still rain-
ing, we walked to the brewery, Only to find that the tours start
at 10:00 o'clock and that it was then 11230, and obviously too late.
From there we ate lunch and headed on our way to Copenhagen.

hours ahead of time, we were unable to make any ship before 3;00 o'clock

We pulled out of town just about 11:00 o'clock, and headed west toward
Roskilde, Actually the only thing of interest in Roskilde is the red
brick cathedral, which is the burial place of all of Denmark's kings
and queens, There are some 40 royal tombs here, and according to the
information that the youngsters picked up in a booklet that we bought
there, there are 120 tombs altogether, including the bishops, etc.,
that are buried beneath the various plaques beneath their feet. The
kings and queens, of course, are entombed in beautiful marble sar-
cophagi. From there, we rolled along the highway through pleasant
farmland with half-timbered homes, the yellow stucco farms, gentle

This morning we were up early and moved out of Odense, again con-
tinuing west, and crossing by island over to Jutland, and cutting

little town of Ribe. Incidentally, most of the farms and homes in
this area are either thatch-roofed or tile-roofed, and the tile is
all red. Today, when we moved into Germany, we found much of the
tile to be much darker, These thatch roofs, incidentally, will
last 30 to 40 years, although today we saw a couple that looked as
if they must have gone at least 50 years because they had quite a
few holes in them. I'm not recommending this as the type of roof
to have, but certainly I was surprised to find out that they did
not have to re-roof any sooner than this 30 to 40 year period,

Ribe has been unaltered by recent centuries, and its key Lnterest
is its cathedral and stork nests, Of course, the storks inter-
ested me, and I find that they work somewhat like the swallows of
Capistrano, for with annual regularity the males appear in Ribe

on the 8th of May, prepare the nests, which are on top of the
chimneys of the old houses or else on old wheels that have been
placed up there as racks for their nests, After they repair these
old nests, they wait for the females who come in some 10 days
later. They stay in Ribe until August 23, at which time they
take off for their home in Transvaal, South Africa. Actually
there are very few nests now, although the bird is protected in

the steeple in the church, where the youngsters and I climbed the

present summer residence of the king and queen, They were mak-

were beautiful. As we have found throughout the country, the

one garden called the Marble Garden, with the marble all imported
from Italy. We thoroughly enjoyed our half-hour wandering through
this beautiful garden, From there we drifted through more lovely
countryside until we found a little spot where we could have lunch,
facing the Northern 3ea, Next on the agenda was something we all
had anticipated, and this was heading south towards the straits,
and a visit to Elsinor and Hamlet's castle at Helsinborg, This is
a tremendous castle which actually was built as a fort. We wan-
dered through the inside court first, and then in through the tre-
mendous halla and courtrooms, the fabulous large dining room 200
feet long, the many rooms with the tapestries, beautiful furniture--
it was much more overwhelming than I had thought it would be. It
is situated on a very strategic spot on the straits, It is very
near Sweden, and we realized that we could take a ferry just a
half an hour's trip over to Sweden, This we had not anticipated;
go we hopped on this little ferry and over to Sweden we went. This
amounted really to being a shopping trip, but was it funl We all
reveled in it, buying lots of goodies, some crystal, etc., and
hurried back to make our ferry home. Arriving back into Denmark
again, we had a lovely half-hour drive along south, through what
they call the "Danish Riviera," It was a beautiful drive, seeing
the lovely homes along this bay. We eventually stopped at what
they call "Deer Park," had a ride in a horse and carriage, saw
deer in great abundance, We wound up finally at the king's hunt-
ing lodge, and Walt went out in the fields to take some pictures

Nach Berlin

We have just passed through the checkpoint at Helmstedt (Dick talking),
and are driving along the Autobahn towards Berlin, Magdeburg is just
off to the right, which means that we are about a third of the way
through Eastern Germany, This is really quite an experience,

We were up early this morning at 7:30--at least, I mean early for us-~
had the typical Continental breakfast, packed the car in the rain,

and took off in a drizzle, I had that we could go in through
the direct route from Hamburg to Berlin through the checkpoint at
Lauenburg. We had heard various comments about being able to go in
this routey some being that there would be no problem, and others say-
ing that we could not go in this way, We stopped briefly at the Amer-
ican Embassy in Lauenburgy but of course, it being July 4, it was
closed, However, one of the young secretaries there was kind enough
to answer my questions as far as he knew at least, which amounted to
the fact that he really didn't know, The only way to tell would be
Go drive down to the checkpoint and find out. This was not out of
our way, and promised to be an interesting trip, although it would
take a little longer since we would be off of the Autobahn, sut we
headed east along the Elbe River, which was beautiful, as we pulled
out of Hamburg. We stopped at a little grocery store, stocked up
with fresh bread, cheese, sliced bologna, cold drinks for the kids,

a few beers for Mom and me, and the usual pastries--part of which we
wound up leaving behind, It's a great experience, trying to talk in
Our pigeon Dutch and they talk in their pigeon English, so far
things are working out fine, however, .

Unfortunately, when we get th the checkpoint we found that this was
not our day. Maybe it's because we had the little American flag fly-
ing off of our antennay but at least we were informed that this route
into Berlin was for Germans only, and that we needed a visa before
moving in and could not get the visa at this checkpoint, we would,
therefore, have to go to the checkpoint at Helmstedt in order to get
this visa, This is the customary way into Berlin from the weét., In
other words, the direct route from Hanover, This being the case, we
headed directly south through Luneburg, Uelzen, toward Braunschweig;
we stopped along a branch of the Elbe River, climbed up on one of
the protecting dykes, set our little card table we had picked up
in Copenhagen, and had our lunch, By this time it had stopped rain-
ing, although it was quite hazy and there was no sun, The trip south
through Braunschweig was pleasant, through a different type of farm-
ing country=-quite wooded, small farms, brick, and we have moved away
from the thatched roofs of the north, We hit the Autobahn and then
headed east, moving along to Helmstedt for our experience at the
checkpoint. It was with mixed feelings (frankly quite a bit of
apprehension due to the various comments that had been made ahead

of time) that we approached this area, I suspect our feelings were
very much like those of any lay individual upon undergoing surgery

ia really just a house, The second floor has 4 rooms in it that they
rent out to travelers, We are taking up three of them and there is

you get a lot of the feeling of the German culture and of the Ger-
man people, rather than staying in a Hilton or the like, One cus-
tom that we've come to like is the use of a German comforter, which
is a type of blanket that you sleep under on the bed, but it's cov=-
ered like a large pillowcase, Inside it is an enlarged pillow full
of feathers. course, these comforters are really great for‘
Mother's and my allergies; but as of yet our allergies have not
bothered us one bit, The family that owns this place includes the
grandmother, who is the type that I would picture as a typical Ger-
man woman. She is short--well, on the pudgy side, i guess you could
say. Nobody here speaks a word of English, so with Dad's and Mom's
German we get along 0.K., but there is a lot of sign language
involved and it's very interesting to see how they try to communicate
with us, This morning they had breakfast for us--the typical Con-
tinental breakfast that we have run across so far except in Denmark.
Here we have hard rolls, German brown bread that is quite hard, coffee
or tea, The girls are drinking cocoa or milk whenever they can get
4t, Also with the rolls and bread, generous supplies of butter and
Gelicious jam, ‘These small German towns are very interesting--at
least the ones we have seen so far here in Bavaria~--where the towns
are #0 isolated that they have to have almost a little of everything,
because the people very rarely will leave these towns for other
places, In our driving around yesterday, we wound all around in

the mountains and were very surprised to come to these small towns
and see quite large factories and many different types of stores,

all on a miniature scale, Also the towns are quite a bit closer
together than in the United states. In many of the towns there is
nothing but maybe two or three farmhouses. Why these are named
towns i don't know, but they are named towns and they are on the
map, although there are no stores as such in these famiing vidlages.

we have been through more of Bavaria and the livelier part of
Bavariay we have just had an inkling of it so far, Our next

letter will contain more description of Bavaria and what we have
geen, Until then, happy sailing.

walt

Forest area it became more beautiful and we could see how it was so
well named, ‘This is a heavily forested area over an extensive period--
rolling hills, with but minimal scattered farming areas. Actually I
have not seen as many beautiful trees in Michigan, Pennsylvania, or
any place around the Middle West or East. Tall, beautiful conffers,
gcattered oaks, and basically a rather rocky, hilly area at the foot-
hills of the Alps. We worked down the eastern road of this Schwabischian
area through Freudenstadt, This is a rather attractive, but extremely
popular resort area without lakes, but with many nice hotels and appar-
ently many local spas. Although we had swung off from the main
Sehwarzwald Strasse because of traffic, we still found many people

out enjoying the holiday. The weather was beautiful--clear and sunny,
with a few scattered clouds. The people were certainly making the
best of this day, and I believe practically every nook and cranny was
filled with picnickers, or those that were out to spend the day and
enjoy the woods, Picnic tables or blankets were scattered along the
streams, along the hillsides, in almost any open area; and the fam-
ilies were making the best of it. Unfortunately we did not encounter
any of the old native dress--that is, the girls with the red pompons
on their hats--although we went through many small towns actually
trying to see them, Perhaps, however, it was too late in the day, as
it was afternoon by the time we were in this region and church was
out, From Freudenstadt we cut west slightly, and then directly

south through Wolfach to Triberg, where we spent the night. We were
able to stop early about 4:30, wandered around the town a bit, did
some windowshopping, and the girls found some souvenir shops in which
they picked up a few trinkets. The hotel where we stayed was about
the same as the previous hotels--rooms clean, large; the beds hard

(to our satisfaction}; with the wedge at the top which, of course,

we pulled out, and the extra-large pillows. We are beginning to get
used to the heavy feather comforters lying on top of us. Actually
they are not particularly heavy, and are not particularly uncomfort-
able as far as warmth is concerned, Only rarely do I stick my feet
out at the end of the bed to cool them off; and they all seem to be
extremely sanitary, completely covered with a sheet and, of course,
fresh sheets on the bed itself. All of the hotels we have encoun-
tered have been extremely clean, The meals have been excellent,
although the toilet facilities are not up to American standards,

After dinner, Walt and I again wandered on the streets somewhat

while the girls returned to their diaries and Mother to some of her
note-writing, and then we all turned in comparatively early.

Triberg is likewise one of the resort areas in the Black Hills,
although certainly not as well known as Baden Baden, I do not
believe there are any baths here; it is mainly the hills, ‘There is

a large pool, although we did not see it. It is beautiful country--
a beautiful falls which actually we did not see since they charged

a mark apiece in order to be able to look at it. We figured we had
seen many falls in the United States; and frankly about an hour pre=-
viously we had encountered a beautiful one as we were cutting through
the countryside. It seems strange to charge 25¢ to look at a tumbling
falis, Triberg is also somewhat of a winter resort, although of
course not as well known nor as popular as the Alps region.

This morning we were up and away in good shape--that is, considering
that there were 5 of us to get dressed, have breakfast, get packed,
etc.; and about 3:30 we pulled out of Triberg.

as apparently we have not been far enough south for that yet. Actually
we have seen practically none of these since we left northern Germany.

The rain stopped about the middle of the afternoon except for scat-
tered drizzle, and we pulled into Tutlingen in good time, stopping
about 4;00 o'clock and staying at the Schlact Hotel here in the
middle of town. This is a rather peculiar arrangement, apparently
set up as a subsiciary to the restaurant of the same name. The res-
taurant is on the main street, whereas the hotel itself, which is a
comparatively small building with perhaps only 10 or 12 rooms in it,
is around on a side street in back of the restaurant. Parking is

in between, so we at least are off the street with our car tonight.
The rooms are carpeted and very Clean, and we have Our customary
set-up of two twins and a single with the W. Ce down the hall and
the bath behind a locked door. I have just returned from a most
refreshing bath; am sitting with a small glass of wine chatting with
you before retiring.

For dinner this evening, since the schlact Restaurant was closed we
went to the Sahnhoff, a railroad station restaurant, This was our
first experience in such a place, and it certainly was a pleasure.
For those who have not seen railroad stations over here, they are
entirely different from those in our country 48, first, they are
elean and neat and second, the trains roll in and out on time and
quietly. The food served was excellent, and through the help of
somebody passing through we were able to interpret the menu so

that Kay and I had venison in one way, Walt had it in another, and
the two girls had pork in an entirely different way than we had ever
had it at home. All meals were extremely filling, and all were
accompanied by the local Spatzle, or noodle arrangement, which they
apparently use in this area many times in place of potatoes. The
sauce, or gravy, that was used to cover all of our meats was each
different and extremely tasty. The youngsters all had their apple-
saft, Kay and I some wine, and the total bill for all 5 of us came
to about $9.00. We couldn't match it in the States, nor do I think
they could match it in any of the large hotels here on the Continent?
and I don't think the meal would have been any better if we had had
it in a real fancy restaurant or hotel.

to keep some of the scattered showers off, i think the main purchase

that we had made back in the States for his graduation present, it
is a beautiful portable job, 5 bands, works on either AC or bc, 110,
220 or batteries, and cost probably half of what it would in the
S§tates--well under $100,00, I suspect Walt is in his room trying to
pick up varibus stations at the moment, because he seemed to be
extremely pleased with this and plans to take it to school with him
next fall,

After this delightful luncheon and our chauffeured transportation
back and forth, we returned to the plant after dropping the girls off
at the hotel to pack, and Walt and I went to look at their displays
and I picked out a few instruments to have sent home. Walt and I
then returnac to the hotel and we finally left town about 3:00 o'clock.

schaffhausen., As we aporoached the Swiss border--in fact, as we were

ports--the girls reminded me again that they had some post cards to
mail that had German stamps on them, Wow that we were going into
switzerland they were afraid we wouldn't be able to mail them. ‘They
were quite puzzled when I told them that we could mail them-at the
next town, and a pit more Of the geographical history, or historical
geoqranhy, of Gerinany was brought out as we went through the little
town of Buefingen, about 20 miles northeast of Lake Constance which,
like Berlin, is an enclave. In fact, I believe these are the only
two in the world, and it points up the fact that Germany is really
far from one country. Not only is there ast Germany and West Ger-
many, but there is Berlin, which is completely surrounded by Hast
Germany, and here we were going through a second little section--the
town of Buefingen--which is German but completely surrounded by switz-
erland., They trade in German marks as well as Swiss francs. I sup-
pose they drink German beer, and they definitely use German stamps.
Mere we got our first glimpse of the Rhine and took a few pictures.
of it as it was a beautiful day, and the girls mailed their post
cards from a German town in Switzerland.

where he will have a similar status, and she will be working in

her uncle, who is a Professor of Music, to the University of Indiana.

Still in Igls

Hie

Today was a rather eventful day. We are all tired. We are back here
ac Haus Kaserer again this evening after taking off this morning and
planning on heading toward Munich. However, the unexpected happened--
that fear which lies in the back of anyone's mind who is driving over
herew-that is, the possibility of an accident. Fortunately, although
this could have been a serious accident, it was not too disastrous.

We were all very lucky. The car is in the garage being repaired, and
all of us are in the best of shape. Now as to what happened, and then
I‘ll drop back to where I left off with our last letter.

This morning (Tuesday) werwere up in fairly decent time, had our break-=
fast, packed the car, and took off under cloudy skies ostensibly to

go north over the mountain range toward Oberammergau, Garmisch, and
ccward Munich, hoping to be in or near Munich this evening. However,
as we were moving along the expressway outside of town (a dual high-
Way with fortunately not much traffic), we were approaching a cross
lane where we had the right-of-way when a lone bicyclist peddling

along on the right-hand side of the road suddenly and unexpectedly
turned directly across the highway in front of me to make a left-hand
turn onto the oncoming lane from the opposite direction. This, of
course, would have put him directly against traffic on the lane where
he was headed, and it carried him directly in front of us. The brakes
screeched as I swerved to the left to try and miss him, and we hit

the curb which was some 8 to 10" high in this area. We stopped rather
abruptly and then rolled over onto the right side of the bus. I recall
seeing the boy in front of the vehicle as we were rolling, but some of
the others were not sure whether he was in front of or alongside of us
as we rolled over. Fortunately almost all forward motion had stopped
at the time we rolled, although Walt (who was sitting in the right front
seat) slammed forward against the windshield with his head, shattering
it but not breaking it (the windshield, I mean), All of our luggage
was piled on the left-hand side or top side of the car; Mary was curled
up in the back seat trving to rest; Kay and Ann were in the middle seat,
We wound up with the women on the bottom beneath some of the luggage,
boxes and miscellaneous things, including the bottles of Coca-Cola and
the few beers that we had in the car. I fell down on top of Walt, but
fortunately none of us were hurt. Walt reached around and slid the top
of the car back, and he and the womenfolk climbed out.onto the highway.
I opened the door on my side and climbed out the top side of the car.
All was certainly mixed up inside the car, and when the top was opened
so that everyone could climb out, many of the little things fell out
and scattered onto the highway alonside of the car. The boy and his

was trying to gather my wits, a young chap. stepped up and spoke to me
in English to ask if he could be of any assistance, and he certainly
proved to be a Good Samaritan. I certainly avowed that he could help,

evo in Innsbruck for dinner, which is where our Good Samaritan

way up and at the top of the respective mountains north and south of |
Innsbruck, It was comparatively late and we were tired. I still had
my cold, although today I do feel much better, so we all turned in.

Mes. Kaserer and found that she and her husband had started this little
Pension at the foot of the ski lift at Ijls some 20 years ago, although
actually the building as it now stands, and the production that she
has going now, is basically new. Her husband was the director of ‘the
ski school, but unfortunately he died of a heart attack after a golf
session Guring the summer some six years ago. She and her 9 year old
son live ‘here and she runs the place: and during the winter I am sure

four-hour run of stxraight skiing. There apparently are a great many
people who make their reservations here well ahead of time to stay
with Mrs. Kaserer, and I suspect it is a great place to stay in the
winter.

SUBJECT: History of Dachau Germany

TO: ' New Arrivals

Dachau Station had its beginning as & dynamite factory in 1907. It
was operated in this capacity until 1919 when it was released to various
private enterprises. . During 1933 the SS Troops entered the picture,
occupied the camp, and political prisoners began to arrive. Because of the
lack of facilities, these prisoners were compelled to build their. om
shelters. Between 1933 and 1935, these shelters eventually became the main
compound which is now the vefugee camp located north across the Wuerm canal
from the Crematory. In 1933, this prison area was sumpland and had to be
filled in, mostly by hand, by the. prisoners during all seasons, in mud often
in water. 7

- By 1939, the camp had grown in. populasion of SS Troops to a total of
10,000. The parracks occupied by these troops are no longer standing, but.
were located in what is now the Chemical storage and vehicle parking lot
in the Ordnance Area. .

With the exception of the two new apartment houses the present Enlisted
Men's dependent quarters were all 8S Officers quarters. The present Officers
quarters were occupied by SS Officers fron the rank of Colonel and up.
‘These Officers had their functions in what is now the Enlisted Mens Club.
Unmarried mothers utilized the present Officers Club as 4 maternity home
where they came to give birth to their children whose fathers were espec-
ially picked, by the Nazi Party Leaders. They were allowed to remain three
months after birth. :

All SS Troops in the Southern Germany Area were commended by an
Officer usually equivalent to our Lt/General. He resided in what is now
the quarters of the 2nd How Bn, 37th Arty Commander. The SS Commander
had as his private domain, the area surrounding the Rod and Gun Club Log
Cabin, comprised then of the Cabin and small lake with boat house and
private picnic grounds. To add to their pleasant surroundings was a bird
sanctuary located in the center of the lake. Adjoining this area was &
large swimming pool resplendant with diving towers, a bath house and a
sauna bath, patterned after those in Finland. - Today, this pool is used
by avid fishermen.

Produce from our greenhouse was only for the use of the Officers
Kitchen. Finance Officers for all SS Troops in Southern Germany are now
the Bachelor Officers Quarters. Behind the BOG's are sixteen vacant
buildings then used as the troop Hospital. Building 2761 of this group
contains a small oven and was used for the purpose of autopsis and vivi-
sections. Building 9B was the medical officers quarters. Goods and

material confiscated from occupied countries was stored in the present

Quartermaster Laundry and adjacent buildings. Most of the golf course
and adjoining motor pool was sumpland filled in by prison labor. ._

Friday, 29 July, 1966
Luxembourg City

At breakfast this morning, which we had here in the hotel, we all

were reminiscing about our beautiful moonlight walk last night. The
lighting of the towers, the ramparts, the walls and the valley, with
the moon shining over the towers was most impressive. Actually it had
been a clear, cool, beautiful evening, and Alphonse knew the way to
lead us a rapid pace as we walked rather steadily for about an hour
over the cobblestoned streets and hillsides of Luxembourg City.

Alphonse was at the front door to meet us this morning promptly at

93:00 o'clock. He directed us to a garage and was able to arrange it

so that they would give our car the 3,000-mile check, fix the horn,
etc., as well as wash it?s but we were going to be without the car until
5:00 o'clock that night. Actually this 1s very good, because I think
under ordinary circumstances we would have been held up at least 48
hours for this activity. They seem to prefer plenty of warning over
here, and the Volkswagen garages are certainly busy.

We left the car and returned to the hotel to discuss our plans for

the day. The decision was that the youngsters and I would go out to
Hamm, the national cemetery outside of Luxembourg, while Kay stayed
to do a bit of laundry and correspondence. This national cemetery is
most impressive with its white crosses row on row; and at the head of
all of them was a simple white cross--the grave of George Patton. The
memorial statues added a great sense of dignity and beauty to this
area, and it was a reminiscent few minutes that I spent there.

We returned the few miles to the hotel in Luxembourg City, and Alphonse
dropped us off for the afternoon so that we could wander around town.
We had a nice lunch at the Bahnhof, and actually we are finding that
our noon meal is running heavier than usual lately, so I am sure we

are all going to gain weight over here. After lunch we took the
streetcar back to the heart of town, and walked in daylight around

part of the areas that we had covered the night before. We also went
down into the Cafemates, which are the caves and tunnels built several
hundreds of years ago as part of the fortification area known as

the Gibraltar of the North. Returning to the hotel, Doctor and Mrs.

-Nies and their daughter, Ann Marie, met us about 4:30. We drove out

to pick up our Volkswagen and were held up a few minutes while they
were finishing this, then returned to pick up the girls at the hotel
and take off for the evening.

Off and on during the day the weather had been first cloudy, then
clear; but by evenihg it settled down to a good, steady rain; and
although we had a beautiful evening ride, most of it was in the rain
and in an area that we would love to repeat in the daytime, since we
went on up to Vianden and the area north of there along the Our River
ana the German border. We all piled into our freshly-washed Volks-
wagen; it certainly looked nice and clean to take off in the rain.
We headed directly north through Mersch over to Diekirch, and then
up to Vianden. One must remember that you can drive the full length
of Luxembourg in about two hours, and its breadth in about an hour
and a half; so actually although on the map it looks like a long
trip, timewise it could be done very easily in a few hours’ time.
The unfortunate part was the weather, as it was raining while we
were going through some beautiful rolling, hilly, in fact somewhat
mountainous country. The castle at Vianden is quite impressive. We

Sample of their unique and delicious ham. This is a delightful little

a little after 11:00, and we were all rather tired and ready to turn in
for the night. ;

Bon nuit.

Saturday, July 30, 1966

This has been another of Dad's days, although I think everybody has
enjoyed it as we wandered around through Larochette and the areas where
I spent memorable days in December of 1944,

Alphonse met us again at 9;00 o'clock this morning, though his wife and
daughter remained at home; so Walt drove the Volkswagen with the girls
while I rode with Alphonse as we headed toward Larochette. Alphonse
had an afternoon lecture to give at the school, so he was going to have
to return at 3:00 o'clock, and we were going on to Bastogne by our-
selves, We went first to Echternach--a town which was badly hit dur-
ing the war, and nothing but a few ruins the last time I saw it: but

it is now well rebuilt, and with a center plaza that is basically a
tourist reception area. The old church has been completely rebuilt
and they were in the process of having a wedding as we arrived, which
added a little novelty to our experience there and removed part of the
stigma Of the tourist stores in this area.

Bulge period, and through a few other towns that brought memories, such
as Consdorf, and then over to Larochette.

the Bulge with him and his parents, and where I first met him. His
mother died some two years ago, but his father is still living; and
although he knows practically no English he was most gracious. We

Tuesday Morning, August 2, 1966
Paris

The Last two days have been busy and it has been late at night when we
have turned in, so I haven't had a chance to bring you up to date on
Our activities.

Somahow we managed to leave Luxembourg City early Sunday morning,
Alphonse again met us a few minutes before 9:00. We had the car packed.
and were en route out of town by 9:15. This is somewhat of a record
for our family of five. Alphonse drove us to the edge of town where

we bade him a fond farewell, hoping to meet again in the United States,
as he may be coming with his family to spend some time; or his daughter
may be coming to the States when she is a bit older than her present

14 years.

We drove west out of Luxembourg directly toward Rheims, as we were all
anxious to see the cathedral there. It was rather slow driving along
the back roads, although there was very little traffic even though it
was Sunday. However, the winding French roads are not as well repaired
as either the German or the Luxembourg secondary roads. It was a nice
day, sunny but cool, and we arrived at Rheims at about 2:30 in the
afternoon. ‘

Our weather, incidentally, is apparently somdwhat of a contrast to
that at home, according to the few reports we have had. All that we
hear from the States is how hot and dry it has been, and we certainly
wish we could exchange some of our wet, drizzly weather or cloudy
weather with you. I am sure it would be of more help to you, and
some of your sun would be of help to us. The days have been generally
cool, and. we have been more than satisfied to wear our jackets or
coats; and I think we have had more than our share of cloudy and
vainy days for a family who is on vacation. Actually it is cloudy
again today, and this morning after sleeping in we are relaxing and
doing laundry here on the outskirts of Paris while we are trying to
catch up on some corréspondence, and then we will be going down into
Paris this afternoon.

But back to Rheims. We drove into town and down to the cathedral,
which is certainly most impressive. It is a beautiful latticwork,
twin-towered structure which is familiar to all of you, and we were
fortunate enough to encounter:an English-speaking guide who was most
enthusiastic in describing the cathedral and giving us its history.
We spent an hour wandering around with him in and out of the various
nooks and crannies, as he explained the history of this church, which
goes back to Clovis--the first Christian king of France. All of the
kings of France were crowned in this cathedral. Napoleon was the
first DBmoeror who was not, as he was crowned (or actually crowned
himself) in Notre Dame Cathedral of Paris. This little jaunt

delayed us so that we were late getting into Paris--something I had
hoped to avoid--and about all I can say is that we have proved a fam-
ily of five can come into Paris at 9:00 o'clock at night without reser-
vations and get accommodations. After studying the map and the sub-
way, Or Metro, plans, we decided to stay in Vincennes on the outskirts.
We drove in here about 8:30, to find the facilities are basically
limited. Three hotels were listed in our Michelon; none of them fs¢
of the first-class category, but all had accommodations. However, we
waited until we had looked at the third one before we found anything
that was half-way satisfactory. We are set up again at the moment

with two doubles and.a single, each with either a shower or a bath of
modified nature, on a rather busy street, Certainly not the best
accommodations that we have had, but well located as far as seeing Paris
is concerned, and for our departure tomorrow. Everybody was tired by
the time we were straightened around. We had not had dinner, so we

had a comparatively light dinner downstairs (Sunday night) and went

to bed, so as to be up early yesterday morning.

After our Continental breakfast yesterday morning we went across the
street to the Metro and had our first experience there: and much to
my relief I found it to be as described by those who had been here
befores very easy to handle and rather rapid transportation. We
were down into the heart of Paris in about 20 minutes. We made one
exchange to get over to the Opera Square, where the American Express
is located, and it was drizzling when we went inside. Because the
weather was again against us, as it is certainly no fun to try and
walk around Paris in the rain, we decided to take the rubberneck bus
trip,,and we certainly had a busy day yesterday. We picked up our
mail at the American Express, and through them I am in the process
of trying to make our reservations to cross the Channel via British
Airways with our car from Cherbourg to Southampton at the end of the
week.

Yesterday morning we took what they call the tour of modern Paris,
going through the heart of modern Paris--Place de la Concorde, seeing
the Obelisk, the Palace, over to the Invalides--originally built as a
hospital for disabled soldiers by Louis XIV; now better known as a
museum and an area housing the tombs of Napoleon, Marshall Foch, and
other well-known French statesmen or soldiers. A guide took us
through to explain the whole situation, and throughout the day she
really did a beautiful job. We then moved on through the Arc de
Triumphe up into the Montmartre area and the Church of Sacre-Coeur.

It rained off and on all morning, and was certainly raining hard as

we approached Montmartre. However, we wandered around in our rain-
coats in what had settled down to a little drizzle, looking at the

few artists who were out trying to paint in the poor weather, and then
into the church itself. This is a beautiful edifice of mixed archi-
tecture, yet quite impressive. The view of Paris, of course, is beau-
tiful from this area under ordinary circumstances, but the picture we
took in the rain is, I am sure, more unusual, After all, anybody can
take a picture in the sunshine, but it takes a little bit of practice
to be able to take any kind of picture in the rainl

Paris is in a clean-up area. They have set a goal of seven years in
which to have all of their buildings scrubbed, so many of the old black
buildings are now turning white. Basically they are scrubbing them
with water only, because the stone is so old that if they used too
much soap or detergent this would destroy the stones themselves. We
returned to the American Express, then had lunch at Pam=-Pam down the
avenue while it poured outside. We decided to again bus it in the
afternoon, and by the time we had finished lunch it had stopped raining.
Another reason for bussing it was that most of the stores are closed on
Mondays, whereas the museums such as the Louvre are open on Mondays but
closed on Tuesdays.

in the afternoon we had the historic tour, including the Louvre and
Notre Dame; and as the afternoon progressed the sun began to break

_ through. By the time we reached Notre Dame, although it was cloudy,
at least it was not raining; so we were able to wander around outside
a bit and enjoy this beautiful building from the outside as well as
the inside. I had not realized before that Notre Dame was one of the
original, if not the original, Gothic structure, using the Gothic
arches in combination with balconies, and was the original church
using the so-called flying buttress. The guide that we had was a
young lady who, as I mentioned earlier, spoke quite satisfactory
English, was very familiar with the Louvre and Notre Dame, and gave

us a great deal of information. We spent about 40 minutes around the
Louvre. Kay could've spent all afternoon there, of course; but basic=-
ally they were interested in having us see the things that most vis-
itors or tourists are interested in--the Mona Lisa, the Winged Vic-
tory, and Venus de Milo. By 5:15 when we had returned to the American
Uxpress, the day was beautiful and it was much warmer than before, so
we decided to walk around for a bit, have dinner in a place that had
been recommended by Alphonse Nies, and then possibly take a boat trip
on the Seine if the weather held up. We stopped at a little sidewalk
cafe and had a drink, then continued walking down toward the Champs
Elysees. We enjoyed watching the people walking the streets, and it
is certainly easy to identify the tourists, particularly the Americans,
the young girls are the only ones wearing loafers, and generally they
have much larger pocketbooks than the native French! We found our way
Over to the Champs Elysees and walked down it toward the Arc de
Triumphe; then on a little side street--Rue Berry--about four blocks
toward the Arc from Rondpoint, we found the restaurant we were seek-
ing, Jour et Nuit. This was certainly a delightful little spot that
had been recommended by Alphonse, and we: had a most enjoyable dinner
at a reasonable price, certainly for Paris. Kay and I had the fixed
menu: she had fish and I had steak, preceded by wine and the appetizer
(I had snails while she had some asparagus), then winding up with des-
sert. All of this for $3.17, which certainly is reasonable for Paris.
As I mentioned, the place had a delightful atmosphere; it is a very
nice place and I would highly recommend it for either lunch or dinner
to anybody coming this way who finds himself near the Champs or the
Arc de Triumphe near mealtime. After dinner we walked down and took
the 9:30 boat trip on the Seine. It was a beautiful evening, although
cool, and the moon came up while we were out. We went down the Seine
and then returned, seeing the bridges and some of the towers lit up

at night. Notre Dame again was beautiful by artificial light, and

the flying buttresses, which are white, certainly stood out well
against the dark cathedral itself. On this trip we saw our second
Statue of Liberty for the day, having seen the original smaller model
in the Luxembourg Gardens in the afternoon, which was built as a model
for the Statue of Liberty as it stands in New York City. The second
One that we saw in the evening is actually in the Seine, and we turned
around it on our boat trip.

ticular difficulty returned to our hotel, turning in about midnight.

things thid morning, as I mentioned earlier. Now as it approaches
noon we will again be returning to Paris to walk around and let the
girls shop while I try to conclude my reservation business at Amer-

Wednesday, August 3, 1966
Paris

This is Walt with the microphone now, trying to fintsh up yesterday's
activities, which was supposedly our last day in Paris. We again took
the subway down into Paris, getting off along the Seine River. We
walked along the Seine in the rain, looking at all the used book
stalls on the embankments along the side of the river. iany of

these places sold more than just used books; many had original prints
from the 1800's, and also many stamps for stamp collectors. Also

some modern-day watercolors were there for sale. Then we split up for
a while, Dad heading over to American Express to find out what he could
do about our Channel crossing, the girls going shopping, and myself ©
just walking around, looking at the Seine and whatever else i could
find. When we joined again, Dad had bad news. The girls had bought
some perfume and smelled like many different flowers, being squirted
by all different types of perfumes after they had bought some. The
news Dad brought back was that they could not make reservations for

us On Saturday. Possibly the earliest they could make it was Tuesday.
So today we are planning on heading to Versailles, the other side of
Paris, where we will take up headquarters there for at least one day.
While in Versailles we plan to see the Palace, and if the weather is
ary we plan on coming down to Paris to see it at night again, as we
could not come last night because it was raining too hard. After
everybody had heard Dad's bad news, we decided we would have dinner

in downtown Paris and then head back to the hotel, where we could turn
in for an early night's sleep, After much discussion on where we would
go to eat, we finally decided just to walk around in the misty Paris
weather until we found an interesting-looking place. After about a 15
minute walk we found a place that looked most interesting, which we
entered, and ordered dinner. Mother and Dad ordered american lob=-
ster, but much to their surprise found out that it was not american
lobstey--at least, not cooked like American lobster. It had been
cooked, but it was served to them cold; although they said it was
different, but very good. After our dinner we took the subway back

to our hotel, where everybody had a bath and turned in relatively
early, looking’ forward to the next day for our trip around Paris to
Versailles, and hopefully to good results from American Express.

early age, hence his many wigs; thus he was well pleased with the popu-

it, he had a great many of them and seemed to change them approximately

At Chartres we had seen an octagonal steeple turn into a four-sided
steeple, but here at this peculiar-shaped kitchen of Fontevrault we
found the octagonal tower base turning into a square roof and then
back into an octagonal structure again, the total being about 100

' feet in height and 40 feet in diameter. The reason for this is
that there are six fireplaces in the eight-sided structure, each
with at least one flue, so that there are about 20 stacks finally
coming out of the tower roof itself, including the central tower--
all of this to allow for the evacuation of the smoke at the time
of cooking the meals. Actually the circulation must have been
excellent, and probably much better than in some of our so-called
modern kitchens. The abbey itself, of course, was divided into
several sectionss a monastery for the nuns, one for the monks,
one for the poor and one for the sick, as well as the state halls
that. were used when royalty visited. Hence the kitchen had to be
vather efficient. Of course, now there is nothing in this kitchen--
merely the structure itself; but one could well imagine the meals
that had been cooked there, even though some of them were simple
and served in the dining hall adajcent to the kitchen.

After leaving the abbey, which is a few miles south of the Loire,
we returned to the river down through Saumur into Angers, which
was a rather surprising town of some 250,000, and then on to try
and find a place to stay this evening. We looked at three differ-
ent places before finally deciding--not because there was a short-
age of rooms, but because we were looking for something a little:
bit more cheery and in a little better condition than the first
Ones weitinspected, Finally we settled on the Hilton Ancenis,
again in a two-two-one combination. It is adequate but not regal,
for as‘I mentioned earlier, most of these buildings undoubtedly
pre-date World War I. We are settled down for the night, the

and are looking forward to tomorrow (Sunday) when we move on into

coast, and winding up some place in the vicinity of Mont-St.-Michel
“or Avranches.
