Schean, France

This morning we were up at sunrise, although actually the sun was
not out, and off to Mont-St.-Michel for an early morning visit,

and it was certainly most impressive to all of us. The church
itself with its beautiful Gothic arches and choir loft, and its
Romanesque pillars in the nave itself, pxesented a queer combin-
ation. However, one must remember that this edifice was built

and re-built over the last 1,000 years, At no time were there

ever more than approximately 60 monks there in study, and it seemed
evident that the medieval monks were not only religious individuals,
but warriors as well, as Mont-St.-Michel is certainly a defensive
as well as a religious edifice. In reviewing its history, we
learned that Mont-sSt.-Michel, although attacked many times during
the past 1,000 years, it was never captured until it was overrun
Quring the last war; but actually it was not under any defensive
action at the time the Germans moved in. Basically it remained a
religious structure until the French Revolution: then after it was
cleared cut and partially destroyed at that time, it remained unused
until Napoleon came along and made a prison of it, and it con-
tinued to be used as a prison until recent years. During World
War II it was garrisoned by some 250 Germans, but it was actually
not bombed by either the British or the Americans. It seems that
everyone has a great deal of respect for this cathedral, and cer-
tainly to us this seemed justified. We wandered through the dun-
geons, past the big wheel,,through the narrow hallways and stairs,

continuing through the woods, and suddenly there ahead of us was a
large archway which apparently is all that remains of the old castle.
After we had prowled around a bit we suspected that this archway
(which really was a triple archway) was the entrance to the castle,
with the castle lying beyond and some of its walls stili being par-
tially intact; but of course it is now covered with undergrowth,
trees and bushes. The area between the bridge and these arches was
apparently the courtyard. This, too, had remaining evidence of
walls, and possibly even some small outbuildings which had appar-
ently been separate from the court itself. One could romanticize
in this beautiful little area for many hours; but actually there is
little here to interest anyone unless he happens to have the name
of Pomeroy. We realize that act least the name originated in this
apple orchard region of Normandy, although perhaps our direct
heritage may not go back quite this far.

This year, the 900th year since William the Conqueror's moved from
Normandy to England in 1066, is being celebrated here. History
tells us that One Ralph de la Pommeraye, apparently one of the
Barons in this area, left this castle and joined with William.
They left Dives in September of 1066 for the attack on England,
the death of Harold, and the reign of King William I. We have had
a wonderful opportunity to review history these past few days,
both current and old; and we are also looking forward to tomorrow,
when more of the things we have read about in books will come
alive for us. One little interesting sidelight is that william
the Conqueror, or William the Bastard, was the son of Harold the
Beautiful. I am not guite, sure what the significance of this is,

beautiful woods and on the hillside among these remains for per-
haps three-quarters of an hour, getting our feet and our pants wet

lovely Orne Valley to the main highway, north through Thury-Harcourt
ana on into Caen.

Tuesday, 9 August, 1966
(Aboard the car ferry, Viking,
en route Cherbourg to Southampton)

This morning we were up again to find the sun. We wandered around
Caen for a short time, viewing from the outside the churches of the
area and the beautiful new university. This town, of course, was
pretty well destroyed in June of 1944, not only from bombing, but
from shelling by the American Ships in the harbor, as it is only

ten miles from shore. In fact, the whole heart of the town was
pretty: well cleared out. As we wandered through the towns today
(some of which I had been in before), we felt that the earlier
destruction had actually proved to be an advantage, because as

the people have been rebuilding, the narrow streets have disappeared,
I must say they have done a good job, and now have wide streets that
are light and clean. We then headed for the coast at Avromanches,
one of the ‘British sectors in the invasion, and spent some time
going through the small museum there. This town still has some
remains of the landing docks and the heavy concrete breakers that
encircled the general area. It was quite impressive. They have
done a nice job with the museum, and although it (like many other
regions of this type) has turned into a tourist area, it is certainly
much cleaner and more respectful than Bastogne. I think we were all
impressed with the quietness and sedate beauty of the beaches and
the way they are inhabited now,

The villages as we moved northeast toward Cherbourg have been
restored in good shape. Certainly the Normandy people are much
more industrious and cleaner than those in the eastern part of
France.

Conqueror, This is a beautiful piece of work, It encircles a

large room, although it is only about 18" wide, and the detail of

this story is really quite surprising. The historical review was

good for all of us, and it certainly impressed me that the preparations
which William made some 900 years ago for his offensive going into

Friday, 12 August, 1966
Totnes, England

The last two days, except for the weather, have been delightful. Yes~
' terday it was rainy, drizzly and cool all day long, and we saw no sun-
shine. We wore our raincoats most of the day, and I was in a syit coat
and sweater in order to be comfortable. We were up and had an 8:30
breakfast of bacon and eggs. I had "white coffee" while the others

had "white tea." Then we drove the mile and a quarter into Totnes and
split up, the girls going one way and Walt and I another. The women
wandered in and out of the shops the rest of the morning. Walt and I
wandered up the street a hundred yards to the local museum, where we
introduced ourselves, and they promptly brought out Pomeroy books and
books pertaining to the castle. We lost ourselves in these for about
an hour, then rejoined the girls about noon. Walt and I had also
stopped at a small art shop, where we picked up some prints of the
coast, the castle, and Walt picked up a couple of prints of the
dastings area to be used as gifts for the Pratts (with whom he stayed
in Tunbridge Wells last year, and whom we will be visiting next week).
We had an interesting chat with the young lady running the shop. She
herself is an artist and does some painting, and apparently her husband
does also. They have a manor house and a studio outside of town, and
she made some suggestions as to inns and pubs for us to visit along the
line while we are here. Accordingly, after meeting the girls we headed
north out of Totnes away from the main highway and along some of the
very narrow hedged roads toward Torbryan, where we found the delightful
medieval Churchhouse Inn, dating back to at least the 14th Century. ©
This was originally built for the monks who worked on the restoration
of the church at that time; they were trying to restore the church
which had originally been built in the 8th Century. The church itself
was interesting--an entirely different type of architecture than we
have encountered before--but of more interest was the Churchhouse Inn,
and we had a delightful lunch there. Their specialty is ham, and while

some pictures of the church and the inn itself, and a few interiors
which I certainly hope will turn out.

great places to eat and to enjoy local atmosphere. And I do mean
local atmosphere, because there were no other Americans here. There
were many British, and most of them local. I mentioned that yesterday
we went to Torbryan on the recommendation of the young artist lady,
and this inn where we went this evening was also recommended by her.

their favorit spot when they wanted to go out for dinner. The inn
Gates back to the 13th Century, and at one time had been used by the
monks as they were rebuilding Buckfast Abbey a few miles away. It is
on the River Dart and the bridge crossing the river, with its seven.
pointed arches, dates from 1413 and is one of Devon's oldest bridges.
It was certainly an attractive and unusually shaped bridge, and I hope
our pictures turn out.

We are back at "The Dawn" now. Kay has just finished a bit of iron-
ing, and the tub is in use as we are all bathing and getting ready for
an early departure tomorrow. We plan to head north toward Exeter

and eggs on toast. Incidentally, we find that the English seem to
like their toast cold. We took off in good time. The weather was
miserable; it was drizzling as we loaded the car, and all the way

cleared and the sun even tried to shine. We went over to Thomas Cooke's
to pick up our mail, did a bit of shopping and, of course, visited the
beautiful and massive cathedral. This is an entirely different type of
architecture than one encounters on the Continent. The stained glass
windows are missing. However, Exeter was heavily bombed during World
War IIT, and the area around the cathedral was particularly hard-hit;

so I suspect any old remaining glass was lost at that time.

Conqueror. The youngsters were interested in finding the name, Pom-

The following I am dictating in Totnes, England, using as references
from memory some. of the recent readings that I have done; also the
bfficial illustrated guidebook of the Berry~Pomeroy Castle, anda
little pamphlet entitled "Zerry-Pomeroy" in Doomsday Book, by Reverend
er, Jd. Odell, a copy of which I just obtained from the museum in Totnes.
I am Gictating this at this time because it may help to keep things
clear in my mind if I ever have any desire in the future to try to
look into things a bit further.

It would appear that the name, Pomeroy, originated in the area of La
Pommeraye south of Caen, east of Clecy, in France, in a section where
there are many apple orchards. Apparently it was early in the llth
Century when people first began to use last names, and they were fre-
quently associated with the work activities of the individuals them~
selves--such as the miller, the smith, etc. The energetic Normans of
this area were not too far removed from their ancestors, the Norsemen
and Danes who had attacked and moved in on this area in previous cen-
turies. They were extremely aggressive, warlike and restless, and
apparently unable to sit very long in a peaceful manner in any par
ticular area. Hence, when William, Duke of Normandy, came along with
his proposed challenge to the throne of England, the land-holding Pom-
eroys were more than willing to move along with him.

William, incidentally was quite a lad himself, and his planning of the
invasion of England (after the double-cross that Harold had given him.
after the death of Edward the Confessor) certainly might bear more
investigation, This channel crossing at the time of the invasion used

| Jalmost as many ships as were used in 1944, and his planning and logistics
were certainly just as clever, if not more SO. It is to be recalled
that he had been promiged the crown of England by Edward the Con-
fessor. Harold had been sent to deliver the message to him, and had
sworn that such would be the cases however, upon the death of Edward,
he (Harold) had taken the crown himself. William, who was the Duke of
Normandy (and had worked his way up from his illegitimate birth to this
category), was, Of course, quite upset by this, and his rugged person-
ality and hot northern blood woulda not stand for it. However, he planned
carefully before making any attack. First he obtained the authorization
of the French king, and the promise of France's neutrality. Then he
gained the authorization of the Pope in Rome, justifying the expedi-
tion; and finally he contacted his friends in the north, so that the
Danes and the Norsemen initiated an attack on northern England. All
of this took place between spring and the final launching of the attack
in September, 1066, with the Battle of Hastings being fought in October.
This was quite a feat when one considers the transportation and communi-
cation problems of the day. The Norsemen attacked England from the
north, causing Harold to move north of London on this "red herring"
venture; then William moved from Dives south of Le Havre with his 3,000
to 4,000 ships across the channel to Pevensy Bay. When he received
word of this landing, Harold, who had apparently defeated the Norsemen
(although it is questionable just how serious they were in their attack),
had to move south quickly. His troops, of course, were very fatigued
ana reduced in strength by the time they clashed with William and his
_ army. Actually the Battle of Hastings lastea@ less than a day; the fate
}of England was changed at that time, and new blood was prought into
the royal line.

Among the knights who joined with William at this time was one Ralph
Ge La Pommeraye, and apparently a brother of his also, although as
yet I have been unable to learn very much about the latter. Appar-
ently Ralph was the boy of the hour--a Baron and land-holder, and from
what I have been able to learn, quite an Army officer as well. I do
not know what happened to the brother, as very little is mentioned
about him; but I assume he did not remain in England very long fol-
lowing the invasion, and probably returned to the Caen-Bayeux area.

Ralph, however, did right well by himself, and as a reward for his
services received not only the land and the village around what is
now called Berry-Pomeroy, but 56 other similar areas in Devon and
two Somersetshire manors. This ranked Ralph as the fourth or fifth
largest baronial landholder in Devonshire, which includes the whole
southwestern part of England. Those rated above him included the
Sheriff, who at that time held a much greater political status than
at the present time; one Juhel, who obtained the property around
Totnes and was responsible for the construction of the castle which
is in Totnes itself; and the ecclesiastical property owners. Appar-=
ently most of the other areas were smaller and not as pleasant as
the area around Berry-Pomeroy, so Ralph decided to build his castle
here. A previous defensive structure had been built here by the
Saxons, and it was around this area that Ralph constructed the walls
and the original castle of La Pommeraye.

When I first saw Berry~Pomeroy Castle, I was struck by its similarity:
both in location and in general outline, as near as I could tell, to
La Pommeraye in France. It is built on the edge of a precipitous
hill with a single approach across a moat. It is not absolutely cer-
tain whether this was a wet or dry moat, although apparently it was
wet as a stream runs nearby. There is a magnificent view of the
valleys in the distance from this hilltop. Ralph must have been a
rather rugged character, and he was most loyal to William. A prison
was established a few miles away, and poachers or those who hunted

or otherwise broke the baronial statues were tried by Ralph in the
castle, then removed to the prison and subsequently hung on what
became known as Hangman's Corner. Taxes were collected in the local
village; Ralph took his cut, the Sheriff got his cut and, of course,
William got his share.

the name, Berry, actually apparently comes from "Beri," referring to
a home or castle, and is not a family name. In other words, Berry=
Pomeroy refers to the home of the Pomeroys.

Ralph died in 1102, although the exact date of his birth is unknown.
His oldest son, William died two years..later, Apparently he was not
quite the man that Ralph had been, and he gave the property to some
of the monks of Gloucester. After his death it was his brother,
Gosselin, who fell into line; and apparently he appeased the monks by
establishing the Abbey of Notre Dame Du Val back in Bayeux, France.
By so doing, he was able to regain the Pomeroy estates in the area of
Berry-pomeroy, SO actually there was only a two-years' period that
the land was temporarily out of Pomeroy hands.

changed very much! These, of course, date back some 2,000 or 3,000

England (which is certainly most valuable to us) guided our tour for
the remainder of the afternoon. We went through Durrington and had
lunch just outside of the town, then stopped for a few minuted at
Wood Henge. This is a much smaller structure than Stone Henge. There
is very little left of the original because it had been built of wood
that has long since disappeared. Again this dates back a couple of
thousand years B. C. Actually the general area around the plains of
Salisbury is studded in many regions with the ceremonial rocks and
pillars of prehistoric man. We read with interest the description of
Azebury, and the comment that it was to Stone Henge what a cathedral
is to a Paris church, so we decided to head north in that direction,
We turned east of Marlborough to the small town of West Kennett, and
then up to Azebury. The town is actually in the middle of the Azebury
circle of stones, I believe all of us were more impressed with this
than we had been with Stone Henge, and came away with a bit more of
belief, if not of understanding, in what had taken place at a time
as Many years B. C. as our present time in the 20th Century. In fact,
Azebury seems to date back about 4,000 years B. C. It covers a much
larger area than Stone Henge, but the stones are smaller (although the
heaviest weighs over 40 tons). There are about 100 of them still
remaining, and they form a series of concentric circles in the center
of which lies the small community of Azebury itself. There are four
roads leading into this community, making four entrances through the
concentric ring, with a deep ditch and earthwork ridge surrounding
it. These are probably the same four entrances that were used orig-
inally. The largest stones were used as portals, and they were found
near the roads that exist currently. In the Middle Ages these stones
were systematically tipped and buried; but during the 18th Century when
the ground was cleared for agricultural use they were uncovered and
many were broken up and used as building materials. As archaeological
interest developed, the remaining ones were saved and reverted to their
Original upright positions. A great deal of excavation activity was
carried out here immediately before the war, and some has been done
since. There is also a very interesting museum nearby, containing
many relics which had been removed during the archaeological surveys,
not only from Azebury, but also from other surrounding Stone Age and
Bronze Age areas that have been uncovered in this region. The sun con~
tinued to shine and it was quite warm, so we had an ice cream instead
of our afternoon tea before we left town, then headed north into the
Cotswold region. Certainly anybody who is interested in the old his-
tory of this area at all would find the short visit to Azebury much more
profitable than Stone Henge, and much less crowded by the tourists,
In fact, the local’ people are puzzled by the general popularity of
Stone Henge in contrast to Azebury, but it is probably because it has
been known of longer and was one of the original areas to be uncovered
and excavated in this region,

ever, it was a beautiful day and everyone was in a good mood and

Blenheim Palace, knewing that it would be closed but hoping that we could get into
the gardens.

To me this was an astonishing bit of architecture, dating back to the early 1700's
when this property and its wooded hill was given to John Churchill, the Duke of
Marlboro, ae a reward for his victory over the French and Bavariansa at the Battle
of Blenheim, The large mansion was built, basically fisanced by Parliament as s
further reward, the family financing only about 1/6 of the coat. We entered the
grounds through a huge triumphal arch, and onto the open rolling hillside where
there were geome cowa and an occasional deer wandering around. There are some tra-
mendous oaks scattered around the property, centuries old, that led to the saying
that it took the oak treea three centuries to grow, three centuries to live, and
three centuries to die.” Historically, the manor ties back with such individuals
as the Black Prince, the fair Rosamond, etec., but the most famous event is that

this ia the birthplace of Winston Churchill, You recall this teking place when

hig mother stepped into one of the side rooms on the occasion of an evening fancy
ball. We were only able to wander around the outside of the palace, which actually
seened to me to be almost as large as Versailles, although of course it is not, and
we were only able to peak at the gardens because they did net open until in the
afternoon. We wandered back through some of the neighboring woods, through the

old oaks to get the general atmosphere. It is certainly a tremendous building

and grounds with the formal gardens, the figured bushes, et al, being outstanding.

We left Blenheim add drove the two or three miles to Bladen where we stopped and
went up to the delightful little church and the graveyard where Churchill is
buried. Through the trees we could see Blenheim in the distance. We had lunch
at a little inn here at Bladen, and then drove the eight miles into Oxford.

Oxford is a busy city of over 100,000 and scattered through the central part of
town, mixed in with the old buildings, are the some 31 colleges that make up
Oxford University. This is a disorganized cluster of colleges, grouped together,
however, 4n an organized manner where therefSAly some 9,000 students, 200 of whom
are Rhodes Scholars. The latter come basically from the U. 5, A., South Africa
and the Commonwealth. Obviously there were some from Germany. The streets were
too busy to drive very much so we parked and walked into Magdalen College and
around ita grounds, with the deer in a natural setting, to the beautiful chapel,
admiring the old tower and quadrangle. This at least gave us s flaver of Oxford.
Students, of course, were not here at thia time, but the city was extremely busy
anyway, possibly from the influx of the summer tourists, We then croseed the
famous Magdalen Bridge and headed out of town southeast toward Windsor,

We are saving Windsor for a trip out of London, so we went down the highway to
High Wycombe because Walt recalled coming up here last year, visiting a gentleman
farmer-friend of the Prattes'. He spotted the unlabeled trail leading back up into
the hills, and ve drove back up on the hillside to thie farm. It was a beautiful
sight, looking out ever their hundreds of scres of wheat and grazing land, but
nobody was home at the time, so he was unable to re-establish his contact, We
then drove on south toward Guildford, skirting Windsor, but going through Ascot.

We were all quite excited as we drove past the Ascot Racetrack and had to stop
and take a picture, being able to walk out into the center of the “green” for this.

Today has been lovely. It was a bit cloudy this morning, but cleared

We did not get away quite as early this morning as we might have liked;
but as I think I have commented before, with five of us someone is

happened to be the girls who delayed us: but at any rate we finally got
under way and headed toward Windsor Castle. I functioned as navigator
with a map on my lap, while Walt weaved his way through traffic on the
wrong side of the road and we got through town, and within an hour we
were in the town of Windsor. Walt had been here last year, and when

he got within gunshot of the place he knew where he was headed, so he
drove into a parking lot and we walked back to the castle. We walked
through the gateand into the cathedral. This is a beautiful edifice;

but is filled with the customary tombs of royalty. Many of these are

of rather recent origin. We wandered through the courtyard and into

the royal chambers, and here we used the tape recorder to good advantage.

Within two blocks of our hotel is one of the well known Angus Steak
Houses, There are many of these in London, and I understand you can
depend upon getting a good steak in any one of them. Certainly we were
most pleased with our entire evening last night. We were planning to
attend the theatre, so we had to eat rather quickly, but were also
desirous of having a good meal. We all had excellent steaks and were
well satisfied with what we had Ordered, and this is certainly a

leasant, but relatively inexpensive place to stop for a steak or

hop dinner,

After dinner we experienced the climax of our stay in Lond, going to

see the British production of Oliver. This was a Gelight for all of us,
Kay and I had seen it before, but thoroughly enjoyed the English version;
and our youngsters, some of whom had seen the movie, and who were familiar
with the music only, were thrilled with the experience. At intermission
it was a bit of a novelty to step outside where hot tea, iced tea or cold
drinks were available; I came back with ice cream for everyone because

it was a bit warm, then we returned to the theatre for the second half
and the climax of the play. The production was excellent. Oliver has
been running for about six years here, and holds the record for the
longest run of any play in London's history. This, of course, speaks

we all enjoyed it immensely. We walked around afterward, down to Tra-

It will be with a bit of a melancholy feeling that we turn the car in
tomorrow, Considering everything, for a family of five who are fairly
close, we feel we have done very well this summer. Only occasionally
have fragile tempers flared; and generally after a short period of

time for reflection, we are all back in a good mood again, I feel that
the weather has contributed a great deal to our times of irritability,
as the cloudy, rainy weather, was more likely to be reflected in our
temperaments than sunshiny days. I don't think either Kay or I has
tried to dominate our course outside of the general routine; and when
any major decisions as to our routing have come up, we have all looked
at the maps and discussed the situation, then moved as the result of a
group decision. It has been an interesting experience for a family, and
one that I think all of us will look back on with fond memories,

This last bit I have been dictating piecemeal and it is now well after

and I think it is time to turn in. You'll hear more from us tomorrow.

Dick

A continued letter--

Continued delousing these Krauts and pushing them in
our three camps. All doctorsand nurses are "frozen" until the
general status of the country is obtained, so they are really

Last night We boarded the train in Lux. city--wait the
city has changed. Its beauty is now in full blossom, flowers,
trees and all. It is one of the nicest cities I have seen over
here. We went again to the casemates (the cities catacombs)
underground tunnels made by men of antiquity with hammer and
chisel. ‘Space for 100,000 people below ground--secret tunnels,
twirling stair cases and all to add to its fasination. Really
Luxemburg is the crossroads of the world, geographically, but
more so typically a beautiful and interesting place and one of
the few places I would like to come back to.

Train to Paris--hard seats, rumbling for twelve hours
over green France. The bright scars of war have disappeared and
are healing as ivy , grass and trees of nature cover up
man's folly. One must watch carefully to see the wreckage in
some places, quite a remarkable change. The peopte are the
same, but now the fields are producing food and they know
it will not be trampled or run over by machines or stolen by
soldiers.

Arrived in Paries at 10:10 and arrangements had
been made thru R.C. to stay at Hotel Orien. Not as nice a
place as we had in Lux. city, but it will do. Called Bill
and will have dinner with him (after I get my pants). Wandered
this afternoon to get the "feel" of Paris. Tomorrow we will
sightsee--although today we did a bit--what with beautiful
girls all over the place--and do they ride bicycles! But

enough chatter--more later.

Many thanks for the pecuniary Birthday presents which
arrived today. They sure will help pay my Parisian debts. I
have just written a rather windy epistle to Alive Mary telling
of my trip which was really wonderful.

In brief--drove, as I told you to Luxemburg. Train
from there to Paris. Four days and three nights of walking
through the city-=no taxis; cabies too expensive for lenthy
trips--subway is a blind way to travel so you walk. Returned
same way with another lay over in Lux city which again fascinated
me. We took advantage of the time and drove up to Bastogne
retracing our route of last 27 and 28 December to where we
sat until the 7th of January. A most interesting and memory
stimulating side trip. Returned via Frankfurt, Wurzberg,
Bornburg, Bayreuth--Hof. All in all it was a fine trip--
but I am working harder than ever now. I took beautiful camp
pictures and when I get them back shall send them on.

Bill was in excellent health and should be with the
set up he has. Really fine, but he deserves every bit of it.
He is in charge of Long Range Planning in communication
so has a good job, detests the army and lives in luxury. He
asked to be remembered to all there--even you Mother--rather
especially you and asked frequently about the new baby, I
am sending him some of the pictures I have of Chuckie.

Am sending a box of pictures home to you and within

love me and Lord give you strength to keep doing so. Likewise
I love you more than any thing else on the face of this earth--
but for gosh sakes don't get the idea I am running around
here winning this war. There are a few other chaps around,
you know.

You tell of reading my letters--0.K., but remember
I am just trying to put into words every day experiences that
all of us are or have gone through. I have but tried to build
up a few people we have met into interesting personalities-—-
as interesting to you as they were to me. But, Mother, every
body is meeting such people. Some don't recognize it or care
and others don't try to put it in words. I just spout off
and certainly am not the Ernie Pyle who meets them.

The letter from Mark Barlvun--blarney and you know
it. Don't spread such tales, please. For instance one of
the captains in the Division wrote home after Remegen that he knew
such and such and worked weth him. Also that Sgt. so and so
worked under him. The connection had nothing to do with the bridge
nor the company that first crossed it. In fact this captain is
not even in the same Battalion and was no place near the bridge. Yet
his fond and loving Mother turned that letter over to the newspaper.
They blew it up, pictures and all, for a spread on the local sheet
telling how this captain's company had been first across the Rhine
The captain was 75 miles back of the Rhine for two weeks after
it was crossed and is not even a company commander and had nothing

to do with it. Needless to say he was a bit upset.

148 Lakeshore Drive, Chicago, Illinois where his Mother and

Red headed, full of life; thinking ten times as fast
as the rest of us; always on the move and admired and well liked
by the whole Bn.--men and officers. He had the most difficult
bunch of men to handle but kept them whipped into shape far
better than most realized until he left. He was full of ideas
to keep everybody busy and happy. He always thought of his men
and their comforts first--then of his and the other officers.
He was a gentlemen and a soldier. An excellent leader. Had
eight tanks knocked out from beneath him without a scratch until
as he said, "I just didn't jump fast enough", When we moved into
Litcabasd he was across the bridge first with four tanks when the
Krauts blew the bridge. We could get no support to him-=not
even infantry for some )-5 hours--until dark, and an enemy city
with its narrow streets, corners, and alleys is no place for four
lone tanks to sit safely. All the tanks were knocked out but.
Batm came out with all of his men. A few minor injuries but they
all came out--climbing over the piled Jerries. The Krauts found
out what a cornered American wildcat is like. And Bagtogne--well
that is another story. Some day you will meet him and all one
can say is "he is a great guy". Bob Crayton back with us now--

good as ever.

We enjoyed our stay in Hof. We worked, yes, but it
was fun and we just had things organized so they would run
themselves, and out we go. The boys had worked hard on an
athletic set up. We had a gym with basketball courts, tennis
courts, baseball diamonds and even a track. We left all that
for the infantry to come to this little village. It is small,
rather dirty and at the moment not too attractive although it
is raining and I am undoubtedly prejudice by Hof. Tomorrow if the
sun shines I will undoubtedly find it a delightful little Bavarian
village, for it is picturesque and surrounded by wooded hills
and a beautiful castle in the background.

Last night I had a wonderful time. The Latvians » Lithuganians
and Estonians at the D.P, camp were celebrating John's Day or
Lirgo Day (spelling???) It is a festive day, the big one of the
year, dating back to heather or pre christian era. The dances
and ceremony has developed through the centurie S, but was stopped
by the Russians. Ordinarily it is held on 23-2) June, but due
to tactical difficulties could not be last week so was postponed
until yesterday.

They made merry most of the day then in the evening had
the main ceremony to which several of us were invited. The whole
idea seemed to be a "open house" ceremony. In their homeland the
people would go from home to home dance, drink beer and eat
bread and cheese. Before leaving the hosts house the gtaste
plant a young oak tree in his yard to symbolize sturdiness,

wishes for a long and true life, etc. In front of each home

joining in the ceremony is a high pole with a bucket of fire hang-
ing from a cross bar (apparently symbolizing life) and in the
evening they all join around a large fire to dance, drink more
beer and eat more bread and cheese. (Beer to keep them going

and cheese to bind them up, I guess--purely a medieval viewpoint
though!) As the embers die down they run and jump across the
coals and if they get across 0.K. they will be married within

a year.

That story I picked up from the Latvian doctor as the
ceremony proceeded, but first I went in with the French Social
Worker (a delightful girl) and we were put with the other Americans
in the front row (about eight of us). They crowned us with
wreaths of flowers and oak leaves; gave us beer, bread smeared
with cheese, and the ceremony started. My wreath weighed a
ton and was buggy so I was scratching and picking off. bugs
throughout, but I guess that was part of the fun. By initially
parting the foliage hanging before my eyes I could see what was
going on, but shortly tiring of this I clipped off the drouping
fronts and had a clear vision.

The Latvians came first danced their folk dances and
sang. The girls were all dressed in their colorful dresses

Crossed the Rhine south of Remagen and to Neswied

for over night then to Limburg in a day where Bamand four
tanks were caught when the Krauts Blew the bridge behind them.
All got out with but minor injuries. Scene of the British
Major General and the P.W's. East to Geiser then north to
close the gap to area west of Kagsel where we met the 3rd
Armored and 9th Army. A couple days rest then straight for
Leipzog (south of Holle), south of Leipzig and circled it to
the north east section to town outside of Tachau. Here is
where I met the Czeck and his folks, This about wound up
our battles, but we rolled back to Jena, where I took a side
trip to Buchenvald, south thru Hof to Weiden and V. E. Day
found us east of Weiden in Waldthurn. Thence back to Hof for
about seven weeks and now Staffelstein.

Chuckie sure must be some baby and certainly would
like to see him. Any pictures are sure appreciated. I sent
the last one to Bill B. as he had seen none.

Went canoeing tonight with Murphy in my kyak on the
Main which runs by here. Really beautiful country. I have
taken many pictures and if you can get any colored 35 mm or
any more colored film, it sure will come in handy. I have
received all you have sent to date and now have several rolls”
of developed film here but am trying to find a projector before
shipping it to you.

Tired, as usual, so shall roll in,

Midwives here in Germany are pretty well trained.
After vital schooling they have three years in the midwives
school and then with their diploma and black box they go out
to do obstetrics. They handle practically all of the OB in the
country, only secondary complicated cases go to the hospital
for the doctor to handle. Occasionally they deliver in the
hospital too. In addition to their instrument bag they have
a commercial standard box (one for each case) which has the
following: (1) 2 x 100 gauze dressing, (2) 200 gms. cotton,
(3) 1 navel binder and pad, (4) 100 ems. Sagrotan (hypol
prips), (5) 200 u. alcolhol, and (6) 2 amp. Silver Nitrate.

Their vital statistics I do not know.

Paris Notes

June 10--Left Hof and went to Lux. city. Wurzburg is
a mass of rubble and many bridges are out. Oh, I will send the
notes may be you can make them out.

Re. the American flags, it has been strange to me
that we were unable to get any standards until recently. We
went through all our fighting without the semblance of aOLd
Glory" and only now that the fracus is over have we been able
to get one to fly over our headquarters. Of course, it would
have divulged our location at times, and perhaps brought down
more fire.

Must rush to the bath as this afternoon Bob Crayton

Bap
and I are going to Bayreuth again to hear ‘itthovan V and Braham I.

If today is like the last two Sundays there will be a procession

by here in about an hour of about a hundred peasants and towns-
folk from 6 to 60 years old. They march by to the tune of a
couple of "umping" tubas, a trombone and a few other horns,
headed by two little boys carrying bamners. They string
through the town all in their regular plain clothes, a few
stragglers with packs fall in line and off they go up into

the hills to the chapel of Vierzehn Heiligen for their weekly
service. They return later in the morning, break up here in
town then all rush to the nearest beer tavern for that golden
refreshment.

at home on Sunday, sit around and read or possibly write. Others
that we see stand on the street corners and chat or gabble away

turned out with their old brush brooms (just like the witches
ride on Holoween) an old basket and sweep up all the manure and
stuff gathered during the week. Then they run around with sprink-
ling cans of water to lay the dust. Back in Hof and in the
larger town of the vicinity manure is at more of a premium and
a poor sparrow would starve to death for the housewives run out
in the streets chasing the horses with little broom and baskets
to gather up the fertilizer before their neighbor beats them to it.

villages where there are plenty of oxen and horses. Quite a
place, this Bavarial

Before telling you of these today will you Send a
check book along in a letter some day. I can use it in a Pinch
now. In your last letter you said you "just mentioned Jack
Payton", I read the letter four times and found no mention of
him so am as much in the dark as ever as to what happened to him.
Story on the White handled knife--when our Bn. went through Bad
Wilmidgen on the way to Kassel they ran into trouble crossing
the river. A few seriously injured Krauts came back to us and
I took off with the ambulance and them up into tow to find a
Jerry hospital for them. We sneaked around the Jerry filled
streets conspicuous by their absence of American kahki, delivered
them and were on the way back wondering where everybody was
when I spotted Col. Kettlewell's peep parked. We stopped and I
got out and went into a building where the civilians were turning
in their weapons. Lo and behold he was the only American there
and having the time of his life. As they brought in their guns
he was looking them over, and the sabres too, picking out what
he wanted and tossing them in one pile and tossing the others
aside. I joined him for a while and picked up the shotgun which
I sent home, a couple of pistols which I later gave away and that
dress knife which an officer gave me. So you see there really
was nothing dramatic in the whole thing, after all. The person
I was referring to made the statement one time that I was lucky
for I would only be in 6 months--remember! My "Time" has not
been coming through the last few months--what heppensd? Time
to eat then I will finish this. Another thing--if you can find
about four "I" shirts, undershirts with short sleeves, cotton,

send them over.

About the pictures--the church spires and steeples
over here have fascinated me. I had been pretty much under the
impression that Germany was a country without churchs or religion.
Yet, I find the opposite to be the truth. True, many priests
and strong speaking ministers were interned in concentration
camps during the past ten years, but religion is far from dead.
Every little town or village has its church and as you wind up
the valleys driving along you can locate the nearby villages
by the church spire peaking over the hill top. These particular
pictures are not good, but I am taking them as I go along and
will have better ones, I am just getting used to the camera.
The one of cathedral spires in Bamberg I took trying to bring
out the clouds in the background but it didn't work out. The
other was of a little town near Staffelstein. I wasreally too
far away for good detail, but I may be able to enlarge that part
of it more. Many churchs, Catholic have that dome like steeple;
a true orthodox, I guess. In the town view, this particular
one, no steeples are shown, but its mate which completes the
panarama show several.

Captain Hulick is at a school this week for all new

officers and I am alone again. Lt, Geyer popped in yesterday
and sure looked good. It is the first I have seen him Since
June when he left us. Hass and Flanders both left last week-eng

Hated to see them go as they were both good boys. Falnders you
mentioned in one of your letters was thinking of Med. school.
I didn't encourage him too much for two reasons. It would be a
long rough ps’ and I fear he might get started then get dis-
couraged and drop it. It would take a lot of work on his part
and I am not sure he could do it.

Last Sunday one of the officers went to Salzburg to
meet his brother and I, always eager to travel, went along.

We didn't arrive in Salzburg until about 2:00 pem. and found

that his brother had waited from 8:30 to 12:30 for him then

left. He wanted towiit and see if he would return so I wondered
around a bit and went up to the old castle. We left about 8:30 p.m.
and drove past the 7s a Nest? and thru Berchtesgaden. Stopped
there to check on our route and found that Eisenhauer and Clark

had been up on the mountain that afternoon. If we had been able

to go through with original plans we would have seen them.

Needless to say the country is beautiful. Salzburg
is hidden amid the foothills of the Alps and one weaves thru
the valleys and along streams going up to Berchtesgaden.

I am sorry I missed Granny's birthday. I frankly
forgot the date and your letter didn't arrive until after the
date. I will write hera letter; really I guess I only write
her about one a year anyway.

Golly, Mom, you ask what I do and still that is about
all I tell you. I don't know how I could go into any more
detail without a minute to minute account. Medically we do
nothing and have done nothing since coming in. We putter around
with colds and athlete's feet and incise a boil once in a while,
but that is all. Now how can I write in great detail about
that. I am letting the Army pay for my tour of Europe! Remember
a letter I wrote a short time ago that you seemed a bit upset
about: well, I read in a recent Bushnell Bugle--"Capt, R. P.
was with the occupation troops, Hq. Bavaria. He was in charge
of hospitals in that country and is helping discharge the
Nazies and passing physicals on them and displaced personnel."

I don't know where that information came from, but apparently
somebody GROSSLY misinterpreted one of my letters. About the
only truth is that I am in Bavaria and discharging P.W's but

all medical officers with Divisions are doing the same thing.
"Hq., Bavaria"--that is Third Army Hq. and I get no nearer to

that outfit than an arrow would to a B-29; "in charge of hospitals
in that country"--Gad--I mst be a full Col. and not know it.
What a story! Read "Feather Merchants" and you may see my
viewpoint and the humor--that is, it would be humor if so many

didn't take it seriously.

articles can draw dow a paycheck for some guy. Points mean

discharge point score, yet) so we should yell}

SEPTEMBER 29, 195

Raining out tonight as it has for the past three
or four days and with the cool wind blowing it is really miser.
able. However, they are tryimg to run up a bridge quartet so
after this report is on its way I may pull on my boots ang wade
over.

Returned this afternoon from a return jaunt to Salzburg
and Berchtesgaden. Bob Crayton and I had planned on heading
further south toward Innsbruck and the Bremner Pass, but with
the continuous rain we just anchored at the Division Rest Center
on the Chiemsee and worked out from that basis of operations.
Wednesday morning we rode the boat out to the island to see
the dream palace of King Ludwig II of Bavaria who made or not
really built a beautiful replica of Versilles. It is more than
a replica for it out does the original. Costing some 30 million
dollars as it stands only l) of the 30 rooms are completed. All
the woodwork and its finely carved designs are covered with 20
karat gold. Let me reminisce a moment.

One walks in the front door into a small room=-the
Peacock Room=--in the center of which is a life-size solid bronze
model of a peacock with gold and silver in the appropriate places.
The hall of mirrors with its 17 mirrors has gold candeloberas
weighing one ton a piece and standing some 10 feet in height. I
don't know how many there are in the room, but there are plenty.
The room itself is 245 feet long by 36 by 2, so you can imagine
its size. The curtains, as in all the rooms, are heavy silk with
gold thread designs and it took some 200 women seven years to make

them for the whole building,

Dear Major Pomeroy:

A committee of students, members of the Advanced Class
at The Armored School, Fort Knox, Kentucky, has been assigned
the task of writing a research report on the action of the
9th Armored Division from the breakout at the Remagen
Bridgehead to the Elbe River. The time covered by this report
is from the 2th of March 1945 to the 15th of April 195,

The information obtained from after action reports is
quite meager. In compiling a report of this nature the
personal experiences of the individual are extremely valuable

questionnaire, which if executed, will materially assist our
committee in the preparation of this report and the determin-

Thanking you in advance for your consideration and
cooperation,

I remain,

Robert J. C. Osborne

Chairman, Committee 13

Dear Major Osborne:

Your recent inquiry about information from the Rhine
to Leipzig is stimulating. I am sincerely interested in
seeing an accurate record of the 9th Armored and its actions
and am more than glad to give my bit--in fact you couldn't
stop me from talking about it if you wanted too. For details
as to personnel, dates and actions you have no doubt already
been referred to "The 19th Tank Battalion--A History" by
Capt. John Sicks and Ed Terrell's classic "The Training and
Combat History of Company "D" 19th Tank Battalion from May
1943 to July 1945." If you have not already obtained these
I suggest you contact Major Crayton of your school.

But you ask for my version! What a story would unfurl
from this old machine if Bamford, Terrell, Crayton and I
were to spend an evening over a few beers and memories,
Crayton would have his share to Say even though he was not
with us at the time. Even without their presence I will
try to give you a few highlights that might be missed in the
routine reports. My source is of course memory, but mainly
letters which I sent regularly to my home and from which
I shall quote freely and without mention. In the search
for more definite addresses of our men I suggest that after
January 1, 1950 you contact John Unger 2 Bismark Street,
Danville, Illinois, who is acting Editor of our annual
communication the "19th Tank Poop Sheet."

May I just start with a date and ramble through my
memories and letters trying to pick out what you might
be interested in, leaving to you the job of definitely
separating the wheat from the chaff:

MARCH 2), -= Left Bad Neuenahr and crossed the Rhine on the
treadway at Honnigan moving into Neuwied, some 2), miles from
the LD.
